Stone_.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019165-147)[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-jeff-148) The album also placed him back on Warner, which had been a distributor of his Word Records releases.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-149) Travis promoted the album in an interview with [WSM-FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSM-FM "WSM-FM") radio host [Bill Cody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Cody_(radio_host) "Bill Cody (radio host)").[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019165-147) He also released its lead single "Faith in You" as a free download from his website.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-150) "Dig Two Graves" was the project's second single.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-jeff-148) In addition to these songs, the album included a cover of [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan")'s "[Don't Think Twice, It's All Right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Think_Twice,_It's_All_Right "Don't Think Twice, It's All Right")".[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019165-147) Jeff DeDekker of _[The Leader-Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Leader-Post "The Leader-Post")_ noted that while it was not marketed as a Christian album, individual songs still held themes of "redemption and the afterlife".[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-jeff-148) He praised the lyrics of "Dig Two Graves" and Travis's singing voice in particular.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-jeff-148) Erlewine criticized the use of a [string section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_section "String section") on "Faith in You", but otherwise reviewed the album's song selection and Travis's voice with favor.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-bend-151) Despite not being explicitly marketed as a Christian album, it won Travis his eighth and final Dove Award, in the category of Country Album of the Year.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-dove-128)

[![Image 12: A bust shot of Carrie Underwood in a purple dress](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/191125_Carrie_Underwood_at_the_2019_American_Music_Awards.png/250px-191125_Carrie_Underwood_at_the_2019_American_Music_Awards.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:191125_Carrie_Underwood_at_the_2019_American_Music_Awards.png)

Carrie Underwood had a hit in 2009 with a rendition of Travis's "I Told You So".

[Carrie Underwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrie_Underwood "Carrie Underwood") recorded a cover of "I Told You So" on her late-2007 album _[Carnival Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnival\_Ride "Carnival Ride")_.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-152) Her version was released in January 2009 as the album's fifth single. Two months after her rendition was released to radio, disc jockey Jesse Tack at [WUBE-FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WUBE-FM "WUBE-FM") in [Cincinnati, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati,_Ohio "Cincinnati, Ohio") combined Underwood's recording with the vocal track from Travis's original and distributed the results to 75 other radio stations. Due to the popularity of the combined recording with radio listeners, Underwood and Travis performed the song together on _[American Idol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Idol "American Idol")_ soon after.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-153) The two also recorded an official duet version, which was sent to radio as well.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-154) With both Travis and Underwood receiving chart credit, the duet version of "I Told You So" peaked at number two on the country charts in 2009, and accounted for Travis's highest overall _Billboard_ Hot 100 peak of number nine.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366,_374,_375-155) The duet won both artists the 2010 Grammy Award for Best Country Collaboration with Vocals.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-grammy-54)

Travis continued to record for Warner at the time. To honor the 25th anniversary of _Storms of Life_, he released _[Anniversary Celebration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anniversary\_Celebration "Anniversary Celebration")_ in 2011.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-allmusic-14) The album consisted entirely of collaborations, on both re-recordings of Travis's previous singles and new songs.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-156) Among the artists involved were [Zac Brown Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zac_Brown_Band "Zac Brown Band") ("Forever and Ever, Amen"), Kenny Chesney ("He Walked on Water"), and [Jamey Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamey_Johnson "Jamey Johnson") ("A Few Ole Country Boys"). Alan Jackson contributed to a medley of Travis's "Better Class of Losers" and Jackson's "She's Got the Rhythm (And I Got the Blues)", both of which the two co-wrote. George Jones, [Lorrie Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorrie_Morgan "Lorrie Morgan"), [Ray Price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Price "Ray Price"), [Connie Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connie_Smith "Connie Smith"), [Joe Stampley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Stampley "Joe Stampley"), and [Gene Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Watson "Gene Watson") all provided vocals to the track "Didn't We Shine". Karlie Justus of Country Standard Time highlighted these tracks in particular among the strongest.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-justus-157)

### 2013–2018: Stroke and subsequent career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: 2013–2018: Stroke and subsequent career")]

In July 2013, Travis experienced difficulty breathing while working out at his home gym.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-damaged-158) He was hospitalized in [Dallas, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas,_Texas "Dallas, Texas"), for [viral cardiomyopathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viral_cardiomyopathy "Viral cardiomyopathy"). While undergoing treatment, Travis suffered [congestive heart failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congestive_heart_failure "Congestive heart failure") and a [stroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stroke "Stroke").[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-159)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-160)[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-rauf-161) The stroke affected the left side of Travis's brain, impacting movement on the right side of his body. Travis was placed on [life support](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_support "Life support") after the infection caused his lungs to collapse, and was declared to have a one percent chance of survival.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-rauf-161) The infection, subsequent stroke, and three separate bouts of [pneumonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia "Pneumonia") led to Travis undergoing three [tracheostomies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracheostomy "Tracheostomy") and two brain surgeries.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-rauf-161) He also suffered [aphasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphasia "Aphasia"), lost the ability to speak and sing, and had vision problems. These issues were mitigated through years of therapy.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-rauf-161) While the stroke largely left him unable to sing or speak, he soon began recovering. According to [Taste of Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taste_of_Country "Taste of Country"), within a year of the stroke, he was able to walk short distances without assistance, and was re-learning to write and to play guitar.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-162)

Despite his stroke, Travis released a pair of previously recorded [cover song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_song "Cover song") projects between late 2013 and early 2014. The first was _[Influence Vol. 1: The Man I Am](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Influence\_Vol.\_1:\_The\_Man\_I\_Am "Influence Vol. 1: The Man I Am")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-allmusic-14) Among the covers were Lefty Frizzell's "[Saginaw, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saginaw,_Michigan_(song) "Saginaw, Michigan (song)")", [Ernest Tubb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Tubb "Ernest Tubb")'s "Thanks a Lot", and George Jones's "[Why Baby Why](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Why_Baby_Why "Why Baby Why")". The only track on the album not to be a cover was "Tonight I'm Playin' Possum", a duet with [Joe Nichols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Nichols "Joe Nichols"). Remz noted that many of the cover songs chosen had previously been written or performed by [Merle Haggard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merle_Haggard "Merle Haggard"), and spoke favorably of Lehning's "low-key" production.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-163) The second volume of this project, _[Influence Vol. 2: The Man I Am](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Influence\_Vol.\_2:\_The\_Man\_I\_Am "Influence Vol. 2: The Man I Am")_, followed in 2014.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-allmusic-14)[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-mayhem-164) Like the first volume, it included covers of Haggard, Tubb, and Frizzell, as well as [Kris Kristofferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kris_Kristofferson "Kris Kristofferson") and [Waylon Jennings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waylon_Jennings "Waylon Jennings"). Erlewine said of this project, "he makes it sound easy when you know damn well it isn't."[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-165) In 2015, he made a guest appearance at the Academy of Country Music awards ceremony, where [Lee Brice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Brice "Lee Brice") paid tribute to him by singing "Forever and Ever, Amen".[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-secretly-166)

In 2016, Travis was inducted into the [Country Music Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Music_Hall_of_Fame "Country Music Hall of Fame"), and sang "Amazing Grace" at the induction ceremony.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-damaged-158)[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-mary-167)[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-168) The same year, he appeared in the music video for "[Forever Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forever_Country "Forever Country")", a multi-artist medley of "[Take Me Home, Country Roads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take_Me_Home,_Country_Roads "Take Me Home, Country Roads")", "[On the Road Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Road_Again_(Willie_Nelson_song) "On the Road Again (Willie Nelson song)")", and "[I Will Always Love You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Will_Always_Love_You "I Will Always Love You")" done to honor the 50th anniversary of the Country Music Association.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-169) Although he had begun appearing in public again at this point, his speech remained limited and he used a wheelchair.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-damaged-158) Despite the limitations, Travis appeared onstage with singer [Michael Ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Ray_(singer) "Michael Ray (singer)") during a cover performance of "Forever and Ever, Amen" in June 2017.[[170]](https://en.wikipedi

**Randy Bruce Traywick** (born May 4, 1959), known professionally as **Randy Travis**, is an American [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") and [gospel music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music") singer and songwriter, as well as a film and television actor. Active since 1979, he has recorded over 20 studio albums and charted more than 50 singles on _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard\_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")_'s [Hot Country Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Country_Songs "Hot Country Songs") charts, including sixteen that reached the number-one position.

Travis's commercial success began in the mid-1980s with the release of his album _[Storms of Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storms\_of\_Life "Storms of Life")_, which was certified triple-platinum by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America"). He followed up his major-label debut with a string of platinum and multi-platinum albums, but his commercial success declined throughout the 1990s. In 1997, he left [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Records "Warner Bros. Records") for [DreamWorks Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DreamWorks_Records "DreamWorks Records"); he signed to [Word Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_Records "Word Records") for a series of gospel albums beginning in 2000 before transferring back to Warner at the end of the 21st century's first decade. His musical accolades include seven [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards"), eleven [ACM Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Country_Music "Academy of Country Music"), eight [Dove Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dove_Awards "Dove Awards"), a star on the [Hollywood Walk of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_Walk_of_Fame "Hollywood Walk of Fame"), and a 2016 induction into the [Country Music Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Music_Hall_of_Fame "Country Music Hall of Fame"). Major songs of his include "[On the Other Hand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Other_Hand "On the Other Hand")", "[Forever and Ever, Amen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forever_and_Ever,_Amen "Forever and Ever, Amen")", "[I Told You So](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Told_You_So_(Randy_Travis_song) "I Told You So (Randy Travis song)")", "[Hard Rock Bottom of Your Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_Rock_Bottom_of_Your_Heart "Hard Rock Bottom of Your Heart")", and "[Three Wooden Crosses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Wooden_Crosses "Three Wooden Crosses")".

He is noted as a key figure in the [neotraditional country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neotraditional_country "Neotraditional country") movement, a return to more traditional sounds within the genre following the [country pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_pop "Country pop") crossovers of the early 1980s. Nearly all of his albums were produced or co-produced by [Kyle Lehning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyle_Lehning "Kyle Lehning"), and feature frequent co-writing credits from [Paul Overstreet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Overstreet "Paul Overstreet"), [Don Schlitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Schlitz "Don Schlitz"), and [Skip Ewing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skip_Ewing "Skip Ewing"). Critics have compared his [baritone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baritone "Baritone") singing voice to other artists such as [Lefty Frizzell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lefty_Frizzell "Lefty Frizzell"), [Merle Haggard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merle_Haggard "Merle Haggard"), and [George Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Jones "George Jones"). Since surviving a near-fatal [stroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stroke "Stroke") in 2013, which severely limited his singing and speaking ability, he has released archival recordings and made limited public appearances. James Dupré has toured singing Travis's songs with his road band. Between mid-2024 and January 2025, Travis released two new songs where his voice was re-created via [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence").

Travis's acting career includes roles in the television movies _[Wind in the Wire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind\_in\_the\_Wire\_(film) "Wind in the Wire (film)")_ (1993) and _[A Holiday to Remember](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Holiday\_to\_Remember "A Holiday to Remember")_ (1995), as well as the [Patrick Swayze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Swayze "Patrick Swayze") movie _[Black Dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black\_Dog\_(1998\_film) "Black Dog (1998 film)")_ (1998).

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Randy Bruce Traywick was born May 4, 1959, in [Marshville, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshville,_North_Carolina "Marshville, North Carolina").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) He is the second of six children to Bobbie and Harold Traywick.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic19901%E2%80%933,_8,_9-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham20193,_4-3) Harold Traywick worked as a meat packer and also built houses.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic19908,_9-4) He also enjoyed listening to [country music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") such as [Ernest Tubb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Tubb "Ernest Tubb") and [Patsy Cline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsy_Cline "Patsy Cline"), in addition to singing, playing guitar, and writing his own songs. By the time Randy was eight years old, his father sent him and his brothers, Ricky and David, to the house of a friend named Kate Magnum, who taught them how to play guitar.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199012-5) Harold also constructed a stage behind the family house, where he invited friends over to hear his sons sing.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199013-6) Randy and Ricky performed publicly for the first time in 1968 at a talent show held at the local [elementary school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elementary_school "Elementary school"); while the brothers did not win, they continued to perform at local talent shows, with David later joining to accompany them on [bass guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_guitar "Bass guitar").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199013,_14-7)

Randy dropped out of school in the ninth grade.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199018-8) As a teenager, he committed a number of crimes, including [reckless driving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reckless_driving "Reckless driving") after he crashed Ricky's car in a cornfield, breaking into a church to hold a party, [driving under the influence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Driving_under_the_influence "Driving under the influence"), [resisting arrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resisting_arrest "Resisting arrest"), and stealing knives and watches from a local store.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199018-8) On his seventeenth birthday, Randy was arrested for [public intoxication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_intoxication "Public intoxication") and faced imprisonment.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199019-9) Despite his charges, [Don Cusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cusic "Don Cusic") noted in the 1990 book _Randy Travis: The King of the New Country Traditionalists_ that his parents still supported him, as they paid his [bail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bail "Bail") and appeared in court whenever he was arrested.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199019-9)

In 1977, the Traywicks entered a talent competition held in [Charlotte, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte,_North_Carolina "Charlotte, North Carolina"), after hearing an advertisement for it on the radio. The grand prize for the contest was $100 cash and a recording session.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199021-10) The contest consisted of eight semi-final audition rounds held every Tuesday at Country City USA, a [nightclub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nightclub "Nightclub") co-owned by Randy's future wife, Mary Elizabeth "Lib" Hatcher.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199021-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-virgin-11) At the performance, Randy played [rhythm guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_guitar "Rhythm guitar") and sang, while Ricky played [lead guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_guitar "Lead guitar"). However, Ricky had to drop out of the competition partway through because he had to serve time at a [youth detention center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth_detention_center "Youth detention center"), leaving Randy to continue as a solo act. Randy ended up winning the competition.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199021,_22-12) Afterward, he talked with Hatcher about his then-impending arrest charges for [hot-wiring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot-wiring "Hot-wiring") a neighbor's truck.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199022-13) Hatcher and disc jockey John Harper, who also worked at the club, chose to represent Randy in court, which led to him serving [probation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probation "Probation") and coming under the custody of Hatcher in lieu of a jail sentence.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199022-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-allmusic-14) Additionally, Hatcher employed Randy as a singer at Country City USA.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199022-13) During this time, Hatcher advised him on his singing and performance. Harold would attend Randy's performances in this timespan, but was later banned from the club after altercations with patrons.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199027,_28-15)

## Music career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Music career")]

### 1979–1984: Beginnings and initial singles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1979–1984: Beginnings and initial singles")]

Hatcher booked a number of country music singers to perform at her club as a means of making connections with country music personnel in [Nashville, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee "Nashville, Tennessee").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199029,_30-16) One such singer, [Joe Stampley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Stampley "Joe Stampley"), agreed to produce a session for Traywick in Nashville. Hatcher paid $10,000 for the recording session and promotion, which was done through an independent label based out of [Shreveport, Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shreveport,_Louisiana "Shreveport, Louisiana"), called [Paula Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewel_Records_(Shreveport_record_label) "Jewel Records (Shreveport record label)"). The session accounted for the singles "She's My Woman" and "I'll Take Any Willing Woman". Traywick and Hatcher promoted copies of the single to radio stations throughout the [Southern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States "Southern United States") in 1979. The former reached number 91 on _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard\_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")_'s [Hot Country Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Country_Songs "Hot Country Songs") charts.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199030-17) After the failure of these singles, Hatcher and Traywick continued submitting [demo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demo_(music) "Demo (music)") recordings to executives but were unable to garner interest at first.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199031-18) In 1981, Traywick and Hatcher chose to move to Nashville to put themselves closer to the center of the country music industry. Despite this, they would still travel back to Charlotte on weekends to tend to business at Country City USA, which by that point had relocated to a larger building.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199029,_40-19) They supported themselves by renting out part of their Nashville house to songwriter and producer [Keith Stegall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Stegall "Keith Stegall"), who used it as an office.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199039,_41-20) Stegall then introduced the two to song publisher and disc jockey [Charlie Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Monk_(broadcaster) "Charlie Monk (broadcaster)") at a golf game, which led to Traywick performing songs for Monk. Stegall also submitted Traywick's demos to various Nashville producers to garner interest in a recording contract. Traywick recorded one session with producer John Ragsdale for the intent of signing him to [Curb Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curb_Records "Curb Records"), but the label ultimately chose not to sign him.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199042,_43-21)

In 1982 Hatcher began managing a nightclub called the Nashville Palace through the recommendation of singer [Ray Pillow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Pillow "Ray Pillow"). She initially hired Traywick to wash dishes, but soon began to have him perform there as well. By this point, he began crediting himself as Randy Ray, as he and Hatcher thought the name was easier to pronounce than "Traywick".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199046,_47-22) Hatcher also rented her in-house office space out to other industry executives, including staff of _[Radio & Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio\_&\_Records "Radio & Records")_ magazine; meanwhile, Randy Ray continued to work on his songwriting under Stegall's mentorship.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199051,_52-23) By the end of the year, Hatcher and Nashville Palace owner John Hobbs financed an independent album titled _Randy Ray Live at the Nashville Palace_, which consisted of ten songs recorded by him at the Palace. Stegall served as producer on this project.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199055%E2%80%9357-24) He also auditioned on _You Can Be a Star_, a talent show on the former [TNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TNN_(American_TV_channel) "TNN (American TV channel)"), in early 1983 and placed second behind Lang Scott, who would later marry country singer [Linda Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Davis "Linda Davis").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199054-25)[Ralph Emery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Emery "Ralph Emery") also invited him to perform several times on the TNN talk show _[Nashville Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville\_Now "Nashville Now")_, which he hosted.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199063,_64-26)

Despite the exposure from _Nashville Now_, he still failed to secure a recording contract throughout 1984.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199063,_64-26) Martha Sharp, then working in [artists and repertoire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artists_and_repertoire "Artists and repertoire") (A&R) at [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Records "Warner Bros. Records")'s Nashville division, attended a seminar in late 1984 where executives suggested signing attractive young artists with a "traditional" sound. Through mutual contacts with Monk and Stegall, she became aware of Randy Ray, who at the time was working on more songs with the latter.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199072-27) Sharp arranged for him to be signed to a contract initially consisting of four songs. Executives disliked the name "Randy Ray" as they thought it sounded "[podunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podunk "Podunk")", and Sharp suggested "Randy Travis".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199072,_73-28)

### 1985–1986: _Storms of Life_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1985–1986: Storms of Life")]

Travis signed with Warner Nashville in early 1985. His first contract with them resulted in the recording of four songs: "Prairie Rose", "[On the Other Hand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Other_Hand "On the Other Hand")", "Carrying Fire", and "Reasons I Cheat". "Prairie Rose" appeared on the soundtrack of the 1985 film _[Rustlers' Rhapsody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustlers'\_Rhapsody "Rustlers' Rhapsody")_.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199074%E2%80%9375-29)[Keith Whitley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Whitley "Keith Whitley") also recorded "On the Other Hand" for his 1985 debut album _[L.A. to Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L.A.\_to\_Miami "L.A. to Miami")_.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-30) These four songs were all recorded in the same session, with Stegall and [Kyle Lehning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyle_Lehning "Kyle Lehning") co-producing. At the time, Lehning was best known for producing [Dan Seals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Seals "Dan Seals") and had also worked with Stegall on his own singles for [Epic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_Records "Epic Records"). Although Lehning did not want to work with Travis at first, he chose to do so after Monk and Sharp encouraged him.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199074,_75-31) After recording these songs, Travis appeared on _Nashville Now_ again on May 17, 1985, where he performed with [Johnny Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Russell_(singer) "Johnny Russell (singer)") and [Lorrie Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorrie_Morgan "Lorrie Morgan").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199077-32) Warner also included him among the performers at their talent showcase at the Fan Fair (now [CMA Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CMA_Music_Festival "CMA Music Festival")) in downtown Nashville in mid-1985.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199080,_81-33) Warner released "On the Other Hand" on July 29, 1985,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-lawrence-34) and it peaked at number 67 on the _Billboard_ country charts.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199081-35) The follow-up "[1982](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_(Randy_Travis_song) "1982 (Randy Travis song)")" peaked at number six on the country charts in early 1986,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) thus becoming Travis's first hit single.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199082%E2%80%9383-36) Following the success of "1982", Travis was booked as an opening act for [Barbara Mandrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Mandrell "Barbara Mandrell") and [T. G. Sheppard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._G._Sheppard "T. G. Sheppard"), leading to both Travis and Hatcher quitting the Palace.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199083%E2%80%9385-37) The song's success also led to him performing on the [Grand Ole Opry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Ole_Opry "Grand Ole Opry") for the first time in March 1986.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199086-38) He also received an award for Top New Male Vocalist from the [Academy of Country Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Country_Music "Academy of Country Music") (ACM).[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-acm-39) This was followed by further opening act gigs throughout early 1986, which resulted in gigs from [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") to [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"). Hatcher and Travis bought a former [bread truck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-stop_truck "Multi-stop truck") which they converted to a [tour bus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_bus "Tour bus"), in addition to hiring a five-piece band to perform with him.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199093-40)

[![Image 6: A head shot of singer-songwriter Don Schlitz](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Don_Schlitz%2C_January_2024.jpg/250px-Don_Schlitz%2C_January_2024.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Don_Schlitz,_January_2024.jpg)

Don Schlitz co-wrote Travis's singles "On the Other Hand", "Forever and Ever, Amen", and "Deeper Than the Holler".

After "1982" became Travis's first top-ten hit, Warner executives chose to re-release "On the Other Hand". Nick Hunter, who promoted singles to country radio for Warner, noted that the song was popular in sales and listener demand despite its initially low chart peak.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199097-41) Upon re-release, "On the Other Hand" became his first number-one single on the _Billboard_ country charts in July 1986.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199097%E2%80%9399-42) "On the Other Hand" and "1982" were both included on Travis's debut album for Warner, _[Storms of Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storms\_of\_Life "Storms of Life")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-allmusic-14) The album was released on June 2, 1986, and sold over 100,000 copies in its first sales week in addition to reaching number one on [Top Country Albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_Country_Albums "Top Country Albums").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199098-43) Six years after its release, the album was [certified triple platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_certification "Music recording certification") by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") (RIAA), honoring U.S. sales of three million copies.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-riaa-44) One of the tracks, Travis's own composition "Send My Body", had previously appeared on the Randy Ray album in 1982.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199099-45) Lehning and Stegall co-produced the album; they also contributed on keyboard and guitar, respectively. Other musicians on the project included drummers [Eddie Bayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Bayers "Eddie Bayers"), [Larrie Londin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larrie_Londin "Larrie Londin"), and [James Stroud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Stroud "James Stroud"); guitarist [Larry Byrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Byrom "Larry Byrom"); [Dobro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobro "Dobro") player [Jerry Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Douglas "Jerry Douglas"); bassist [David Hungate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hungate "David Hungate"); and backing vocals from Lehning, [Baillie & the Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baillie_&_the_Boys "Baillie & the Boys"), [Paul Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Davis_(singer) "Paul Davis (singer)"), and [Paul Overstreet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Overstreet "Paul Overstreet").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-46) The album produced another number-one in "[Diggin' Up Bones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diggin'_Up_Bones "Diggin' Up Bones")" in late 1986, and a number two single in "[No Place Like Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Place_Like_Home_(Randy_Travis_song) "No Place Like Home (Randy Travis song)")" in early 1987. Overstreet wrote "On the Other Hand" with [Don Schlitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Schlitz "Don Schlitz"), "Diggin' Up Bones" with [Nat Stuckey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nat_Stuckey "Nat Stuckey"), and "No Place Like Home" by himself.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) The latter was also Travis's first single to be promoted through a [music video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video "Music video").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990116%E2%80%93117-47)

In late 1986, Travis was asked to host the [Country Music Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Music_Association "Country Music Association") (CMA) Awards telecast to replace original host [Ricky Skaggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Skaggs "Ricky Skaggs"), who had to back out after his son was hospitalized with a neck injury.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990109,_110-48) Travis won the Horizon Award (now called Best New Artist) at that ceremony, while also receiving a nomination for Male Vocalist of the Year. Additionally, "On the Other Hand" was nominated for Single of the Year and _Storms of Life_ for Album of the Year.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-cma-49) On November 15, 1986, Travis performed a concert with [George Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Jones "George Jones") and [Patty Loveless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patty_Loveless "Patty Loveless") in Charlotte, North Carolina, where Charlotte's then-mayor [Harvey Gantt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Gantt "Harvey Gantt") declared November 15 to be "Randy Travis Day". A similar acknowledgement was passed as a city ordinanace in Travis's hometown of Marshville soon afterward.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990112-50) Warner also issued a Christmas single in December 1986 titled "White Christmas Makes Me Blue", which sold over 79,000 copies.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990114-51) By year's end, Skaggs had inducted Travis into the Grand Ole Opry.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990115-52) "Diggin' Up Bones" also accounted for Travis's first [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award") nomination, in the category of [Best Male Country Vocal Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Male_Country_Vocal_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Male Country Vocal Performance"), in early 1987.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990121,_122-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-grammy-54)

_Storms of Life_ received critical favor. Mark A. Humphrey of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") wrote that Travis had "astonishing [Lefty Frizzell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lefty_Frizzell "Lefty Frizzell")-style pipes, excellent material, and sympathetic production".[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-storms_of_life-55) An uncredited review in _Billboard_ also described Travis's voice with favor, additionally stating that " He has the material—introspective lyrics and gorgeous melodies—and the understated, classic country production here to make the most of his gifts."[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-56) Writing for the _[Chicago Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago\_Tribune "Chicago Tribune")_, Jack Hurst also compared Travis's voice favorably to both Frizzell and [Merle Haggard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merle_Haggard "Merle Haggard"), while also praising the lyrics of the singles in particular.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-57)

### 1987–1988: _Always & Forever_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1987–1988: Always & Forever")]

In early 1987, Travis released the single "[Forever and Ever, Amen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forever_and_Ever,_Amen "Forever and Ever, Amen")". It held the number-one position on the _Billboard_ country charts for three weeks,[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990122-58) becoming the first song to hold that position for that long since [Johnny Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Lee_(singer) "Johnny Lee (singer)")'s "[Lookin' for Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lookin'_for_Love "Lookin' for Love")" in 1980.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoland1991490-59) The song served as the lead single to his second Warner album _[Always & Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Always\_&\_Forever\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Always & Forever (Randy Travis album)")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-allmusic-14) As with "On the Other Hand", Schlitz and Overstreet co-wrote the song.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Corresponding with this song's success, Travis won Male Vocalist of the Year from the ACM awards, where _Storms of Life_ won Album of the Year and "On the Other Hand" won both Song and Single of the Year.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-acm-39) During the awards ceremony, Travis performed "Forever and Ever, Amen" live for the first time. Cusic described the song in 1990 as a "career record".[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990122-58) In addition to topping the country charts, "Forever and Ever, Amen" was a minor hit single in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), reaching number 55 on the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-60) In 2019, editors of _[The Tennessean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Tennessean "The Tennessean")_ listed it as one of the 100 greatest country songs of all time, while also referring to it as Travis's [signature song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signature_song "Signature song").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-61) "Forever and Ever, Amen" is also Travis's highest-certified single, having earned double-platinum RIAA certification in 2021.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-riaa-44)

[![Image 7: Randy Travis, wearing a gray suit while singing into a microphone](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Randy_Travis_MCI_Center_In_Washington.jpg/250px-Randy_Travis_MCI_Center_In_Washington.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Randy_Travis_MCI_Center_In_Washington.jpg)

Travis performing in 2003

_Always & Forever_ included Lehning as producer, with many of the same vocal and instrumental contributors as its predecessor such as Baillie & the Boys, Douglas, and Overstreet.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-62) Lehning worked with Travis, Hatcher, and Sharp to pick from several hundred songs before determining which ones would appear on the album.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990124-63) One track on the album was [Dennis Linde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Linde "Dennis Linde")'s composition "[What'll You Do About Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What'll_You_Do_About_Me "What'll You Do About Me")",[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990123-64) which was previously released by [Steve Earle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Earle "Steve Earle") in 1984;[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-earle-65) the song would later be released by [the Forester Sisters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Forester_Sisters "The Forester Sisters") in 1992,[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017130-66) and [Doug Supernaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doug_Supernaw "Doug Supernaw") in 1995.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017353-67) During the promotion of the album, Travis began to notice strain on his vocal cords, which was treated through consultations at [Vanderbilt University Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanderbilt_University_Medical_Center "Vanderbilt University Medical Center").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990125-68)_Always & Forever_ spent 43 weeks at the top of the _Billboard_[Top Country Albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_Country_Albums "Top Country Albums") charts, breaking the previous longevity record of 28 weeks set by [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama_(band) "Alabama (band)")'s _[Mountain Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain\_Music\_(Alabama\_album) "Mountain Music (Alabama album)")_ earlier in the decade.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoland1991490-59)

"[I Won't Need You Anymore (Always and Forever)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Won't_Need_You_Anymore_(Always_and_Forever) "I Won't Need You Anymore (Always and Forever)")", "[Too Gone Too Long](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Too_Gone_Too_Long "Too Gone Too Long")", and "[I Told You So](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Told_You_So_(Randy_Travis_song) "I Told You So (Randy Travis song)")" were all released as singles from _Always & Forever_, with all three reaching number one on the _Billboard_ country charts between 1987 and 1988.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Travis wrote "I Told You So" by himself in 1982 around the time he attempted to sign with Curb Records. Monk submitted the song to [Lee Greenwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Greenwood "Lee Greenwood") at that time, although he declined it. Both [Darrell Clanton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darrell_Clanton "Darrell Clanton") and Barbara Mandrell had recorded the song,[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199042,_43,_63,_81-69) the former as the [B-side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-side "B-side") of his 1985 single "I Forgot That I Don't Live Here Anymore".[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn201783-70) In 1996, _Always & Forever_ received Travis's highest certification of quintuple platinum for sales of five million copies.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-riaa-44)

_Always & Forever_ and its singles accounted for several award wins and nominations for Travis. "Forever and Ever, Amen" won both Song and Single of the Year at the following year's ACM awards (honoring the year 1987), where Travis also won Top Male Vocalist. He was also nominated for Entertainer of the Year, while "Forever and Ever, Amen" received a Music Video of the Year nomination and _Always & Forever_ was nominated for Album of the Year.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-acm-39) At the 1987 CMA Awards, Travis won Male Vocalist of the Year and was nominated for Entertainer of the Year while "Forever and Ever, Amen" won Single of the Year and was nominated for Music Video of the Year and _Always & Forever_ won Album of the Year.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-cma-49) Additionally, _Always & Forever_ accounted for Travis's first Grammy Award win, for Best Male Country Vocal Performance at the [30th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/30th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "30th Annual Grammy Awards") in March 1988.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-grammy-54)[Stephen Thomas Erlewine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Thomas_Erlewine "Stephen Thomas Erlewine"), writing for AllMusic, thought the album "rivaled its predecessor in its quality" while also stating that it had "lean" production and "nuanced" vocals.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-71)

### 1988–1990: _Old 8×10_ and _No Holdin' Back_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1988–1990: Old 8×10 and No Holdin' Back")]

Travis continued to tour throughout the United States in 1988, including a spot on the [Marlboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlboro "Marlboro") Country Music Tour in [Madison Square Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Square_Garden "Madison Square Garden"), which also featured Alabama, [the Judds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Judds "The Judds"), and [George Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Strait "George Strait").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990150-72) That same year he released his third Warner album, _[Old 8×10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old\_8%C3%9710 "Old 8×10")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-allmusic-14) The album was originally slated to be released on July 12, but was moved up to June 30 to make it eligible for CMA Awards.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990152-73) The first three singles off the album all went to number one on the country charts between 1988 and early 1989. These were "[Honky Tonk Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honky_Tonk_Moon "Honky Tonk Moon")", "[Deeper Than the Holler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deeper_Than_the_Holler "Deeper Than the Holler")" (another Overstreet-Schlitz collaboration), and "[Is It Still Over?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is_It_Still_Over%3F "Is It Still Over?")"[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) The fourth and final single, "[Promises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promises_(Randy_Travis_song) "Promises (Randy Travis song)")" (which Travis wrote with John Lindley), was much less successful with a number 17 peak on Hot Country Songs.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Music journalists Tom Roland and [Colin Larkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Larkin "Colin Larkin") both attributed the song's failure to it featuring just vocals and acoustic guitar.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoland1991569,_570-74)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-virgin-11)_Old 8×10_ became his third consecutive album to reach the number one position on Top Country Albums.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-Country_Albums-75) It also won Travis a Grammy Award for Best Male Country Vocal Performance.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-grammy-54) "I Told You So" received a Single of the Year nomination from the Academy of Country Music, while Travis himself was nominated as both Entertainer of the Year and Top Male Vocalist in 1988 and 1989.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-acm-39) Also in 1988, the Country Music Association awarded him as Male Vocalist of the Year a second time, along with an Entertainer of the Year nomination, as well as Single and Song of the Year nominations for "I Told You So".[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-cma-49) The foundation also nominated _Old 8×10_ for Album of the Year alongside additional Male Vocalist and Entertainer of the Year nominations.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-cma-49) Reviewing the album for AllMusic, [Brian Mansfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Mansfield "Brian Mansfield") stated that it "lacks the monster hits of his debut but wears just as well."[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-76) In 1997, _Old 8×10_ received its highest certification of double-platinum.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-riaa-44)

[![Image 8: A black-and-white headshot of Brook Benton](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Brook_Benton_1959.jpg/250px-Brook_Benton_1959.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brook_Benton_1959.jpg)

Travis had a hit single in 1989 with a cover of "It's Just a Matter of Time", originally by Brook Benton (pictured in 1959).

Travis ended 1989 with two studio albums. First was a Christmas album titled _[An Old Time Christmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An\_Old\_Time\_Christmas "An Old Time Christmas")_, which included the previously released Christmas single "White Christmas Makes Me Blue". The other tracks included a mix of Christmas standards and original songs, one of which ("How Do I Wrap My Heart Up for Christmas") Travis co-wrote with Overstreet.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-77) A month later was the studio release _[No Holdin' Back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No\_Holdin'\_Back "No Holdin' Back")_. Prior to the album's release, Travis had recorded a cover of [Brook Benton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brook_Benton "Brook Benton")'s "[It's Just a Matter of Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Just_a_Matter_of_Time_(song) "It's Just a Matter of Time (song)")" with producer [Richard Perry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Perry "Richard Perry") for a covers album titled _Rock, Rhythm & Blues_. Because he liked the sound of the recording, he chose to include it on _No Holdin' Back_ as the album's first single. The rendition reached number one on the country charts in December 1989.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoland1991569%E2%80%93570-78) At the [32nd Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/32nd_Annual_Grammy_Awards "32nd Annual Grammy Awards"), this rendition was nominated for Best Male Country Vocal Performance.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-grammy-54) After the "It's Just a Matter of Time" cover came "[Hard Rock Bottom of Your Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_Rock_Bottom_of_Your_Heart "Hard Rock Bottom of Your Heart")". Written by [Hugh Prestwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Prestwood "Hugh Prestwood"), the song held the number one position on _Billboard_ Hot Country Songs for four weeks, accounting for Travis's longest stay at that position.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-allmusic-14) The third and final single from _No Holdin' Back_ was "[He Walked on Water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/He_Walked_on_Water "He Walked on Water")", which peaked at number two.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) The song was the first successful cut for songwriter [Allen Shamblin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_Shamblin "Allen Shamblin").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-79) Also included on _No Holdin' Back_ were a cover of [Marty Robbins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Robbins "Marty Robbins")' "[Singing the Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singing_the_Blues "Singing the Blues")" and the track "[Somewhere in My Broken Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somewhere_in_My_Broken_Heart "Somewhere in My Broken Heart")", later a single for its co-writer [Billy Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Dean "Billy Dean").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017105-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-holdin-81) Thom Jurek's review for AllMusic praised Travis's vocal deliveries on "It's Just a Matter of Time" and "Hard Rock Bottom of Your Heart" while also calling Lehning's production "flawless".[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-holdin-81) In a review for _[Cash Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cash\_Box "Cash Box")_ magazine, Kimmy Wix described "He Walked on Water" as having "detailed lyrics to which we can all relate" and thought the song was well suited for Travis's voice.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-cashbox-82)

### 1990–1992: _Heroes & Friends_, _High Lonesome_, and greatest-hits albums

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1990–1992: Heroes & Friends, High Lonesome, and greatest-hits albums")]

Travis's first album to be released in the 1990s was _[Heroes & Friends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heroes\_&\_Friends "Heroes & Friends")_, a duets album. Among the duet artists featured were [Tammy Wynette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tammy_Wynette "Tammy Wynette"), [Merle Haggard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merle_Haggard "Merle Haggard"), [George Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Jones "George Jones"), [B. B. King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._B._King "B. B. King"), and [Clint Eastwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clint_Eastwood "Clint Eastwood").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-virgin-11) According to journalist Gary Graff, Travis had wanted to record a duet album for several years, and he and Hatcher spent over a year and a half arranging for the recording sessions.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-graff-83) The album accounted for two singles in "[A Few Ole Country Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Few_Ole_Country_Boys "A Few Ole Country Boys")" (a duet with Jones) and title track "[Heroes and Friends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heroes_and_Friends "Heroes and Friends")" (the only track on the album not to be a duet). Both songs peaked within the top 10 of the country charts between late 1990 and early 1991.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Travis performed "Heroes and Friends" at the 1991 CMA Awards telecast, joined by Jones, Wynette, [Vern Gosdin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vern_Gosdin "Vern Gosdin"), and [Roy Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Rogers "Roy Rogers").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019123-84) Unlike his previous albums, _Heroes & Friends_ was met with mixed reception from critics. _[Austin American-Statesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin\_American-Statesman "Austin American-Statesman")_ writer Lee Nichols thought that the album's songs were "not particularly notable, but nonetheless enjoyable".[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-85)[Knight Ridder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight_Ridder "Knight Ridder") writer Dan DeLuca (in a review re-published in _[The Anniston Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Anniston\_Star "The Anniston Star")_) praised the duets with Haggard and Jones, and considered the duet version of [Dolly Parton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolly_Parton "Dolly Parton")'s "[Do I Ever Cross Your Mind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Do_I_Ever_Cross_Your_Mind "Do I Ever Cross Your Mind")" to be the strongest track, although he also panned the contributions of King and Eastwood.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-86) In a review for _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment\_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_, [Alanna Nash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alanna_Nash "Alanna Nash") thought that "[t]he guests show up more to bolster Travis's profile than to actually perform full-out", although she praised [Loretta Lynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loretta_Lynn "Loretta Lynn")'s duet vocals on "Shopping for Dresses".[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-87) Despite the mixed reception, _Heroes & Friends_ certified platinum in 1991.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-riaa-44) Travis also noted that 1990 was the first year in which he did not receive any ACM or CMA awards, but that he was still receiving significant radio airplay and sales, and positive feedback from fans in concert.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-graff-83) Relatedly, Mansfield and [Colin Larkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Larkin "Colin Larkin") both observed that in the early 1990s, Travis's success began to diminish as newer artists such as [Clint Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clint_Black "Clint Black") and [Garth Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garth_Brooks "Garth Brooks") grew in popularity.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-allmusic-14)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-virgin-11)

[![Image 9: A head shot of Alan Jackson, wearing a cowboy hat and sunglasses](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/AlanJacksonApr10.jpg/250px-AlanJacksonApr10.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AlanJacksonApr10.jpg)

Alan Jackson co-wrote several songs on Travis's 1991 album _High Lonesome_.

Travis's next studio album was 1991's _[High Lonesome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High\_Lonesome\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "High Lonesome (Randy Travis album)")_, led off by the single "[Point of Light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_of_Light "Point of Light")".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1)[George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush"), then [President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States"), commissioned Schlitz and [Thom Schuyler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thom_Schuyler "Thom Schuyler") to write the song as a tie-in to his "[thousand points of light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thousand_points_of_light "Thousand points of light")" campaign for [volunteerism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volunteerism "Volunteerism").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019115-88) Because of its inspiration, Travis noted that journalists often asked him about political matters, and he refused to answer them as he did not think the song itself was political.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-89) He also performed the song for a number of events intended to honor American soldiers returning from [Operation Desert Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Desert_Storm "Operation Desert Storm").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019115,_116-90) Next from _High Lonesome_ was Travis's twelfth number-one, "[Forever Together](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forever_Together "Forever Together")",[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) one of several songs he wrote with [Alan Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Jackson "Alan Jackson") while the two were on tour together in 1991.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-bernard-91) These collaborations also produced the album's next two singles "[Better Class of Losers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Better_Class_of_Losers "Better Class of Losers")" and "[I'd Surrender All](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'd_Surrender_All "I'd Surrender All")" between late 1991 and early 1992, as well as Jackson's number one single "[She's Got the Rhythm (And I Got the Blues)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/She's_Got_the_Rhythm_(And_I_Got_the_Blues) "She's Got the Rhythm (And I Got the Blues)")" later in 1992.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019124-92) Jackson also co-wrote the track "Allergic to the Blues", while Travis wrote "I'm Gonna Have a Little Talk" (featuring backing vocals from gospel group [Take 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take_6 "Take 6")[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-jurek_high-93)) and "Oh, What a Time to Be Me". Travis noted that the project contained more songs written by him than his previous ones did.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-bernard-91) Jurek praised the Jackson co-writes in particular, highlighting their lyrics and vocal deliveries in his review for AllMusic.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-jurek_high-93) Nash also praised the lyrics on the songs co-written by Jackson, while also stating that Travis "never sounded so relaxed or so confident".[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-nash_lonesome-94)

Later the same year, Warner released a pair of [greatest hits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest_hits "Greatest hits") albums: _[Greatest Hits, Volume One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest\_Hits,\_Volume\_One\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Greatest Hits, Volume One (Randy Travis album)")_ and _[Greatest Hits, Volume Two](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest\_Hits,\_Volume\_Two\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Greatest Hits, Volume Two (Randy Travis album)")_. In addition to featuring most of his hit singles to this point, the projects also included four new tracks and the album cut "Reasons I Cheat" from _Storms of Life_.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-beyer-95) Among the new tracks, "[If I Didn't Have You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_I_Didn't_Have_You_(Randy_Travis_song) "If I Didn't Have You (Randy Travis song)")" and "[Look Heart, No Hands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Look_Heart,_No_Hands "Look Heart, No Hands")" both went to number one upon release as singles that year. [Skip Ewing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skip_Ewing "Skip Ewing") and [Max D. Barnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_D._Barnes "Max D. Barnes") wrote the former, while [Trey Bruce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trey_Bruce "Trey Bruce") and [Russell Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Smith_(singer) "Russell Smith (singer)") wrote the latter.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Despite these songs' successes on radio, their follow-up "[An Old Pair of Shoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Old_Pair_of_Shoes "An Old Pair of Shoes")" reached number 21 upon release in early 1993.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Both greatest-hits albums certified platinum in 1995.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-riaa-44)

### 1992–1995: _Wind in the Wire_ and _This Is Me_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 1992–1995: Wind in the Wire and This Is Me")]

Travis took a hiatus from touring in 1992 and 1993, citing exhaustion as the reason for doing so.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019126-96) He and Hatcher chose to spend time at a property in [Maui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui "Maui") they had acquired. According to Travis, the touring hiatus caused some fans and news reporters to believe he had retired,[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-new_album-97) so his publicists issued press releases indicating he was "merely taking a break".[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019127-98) During the hiatus, he released an album of [Western music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_music_(North_America) "Western music (North America)") titled _[Wind in the Wire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind\_in\_the\_Wire "Wind in the Wire")_, a tie-in to a television movie [of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_in_the_Wire_(film) "Wind in the Wire (film)") in which he starred.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-allmusic-14) The album was produced by session guitarist Steve Gibson, making it his first since the Randy Ray album not to be produced by Kyle Lehning.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019130-99) It was commercially unsuccessful, with none of its singles reaching top 40 on the _Billboard_ charts.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-allmusic-14) However, lead single "[Cowboy Boogie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowboy_Boogie "Cowboy Boogie")" reached number 10 on the Canadian country music charts then published by _[RPM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RPM\_(magazine) "RPM (magazine)")_.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-100) Travis and one of his managers later attributed the album's commercial failure to its [Western swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_swing "Western swing") sound proving unpopular with radio.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-new_album-97)

In late 1993, Travis began working on a follow-up album with Lehning when he was contacted by a representative for the then-under construction [MGM Grand Las Vegas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MGM_Grand_Las_Vegas "MGM Grand Las Vegas") in [Las Vegas, Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Vegas,_Nevada "Las Vegas, Nevada"). The representative wanted Travis to be the first country artist to perform at the new venue once it opened, which inspired Travis to begin touring again. He and Hatcher joined with Jeff Davis, another former manager of Travis's who was then working with [Brother Phelps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brother_Phelps "Brother Phelps"), to assemble a backing band for the Las Vegas shows, which included Lehning as keyboardist.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019131,_132-101) The Las Vegas shows, held in early 1994, were his first concerts in over 14 months.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-new_album-97) Due to the success of these shows, Travis resumed his touring schedule soon afterward. He re-established his existing touring band and performed at a showcase of Warner Bros. artists held in Nashville during the Country Radio Seminar, an annual promotional concert series held by [Country Radio Broadcasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Radio_Broadcasters "Country Radio Broadcasters").[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019131,_132-101)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-new_album-97) At the same time, Travis continued writing and compiling songs for his next studio album. "[Before You Kill Us All](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Before_You_Kill_Us_All "Before You Kill Us All")" was released on February 28, 1994,[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-new_album-97) as the lead single to his next Warner album _[This Is Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This\_Is\_Me\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "This Is Me (Randy Travis album)")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-allmusic-14) The song peaked at number two on the _Billboard_ country charts.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Travis and Lehning chose the song because the two wanted "story songs and some with a wink of humor".[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019133-102) Similarly, he told _Billboard_ in 1994 that the song was an example of a more modern and "rowdy" sound he wanted to achieve relative to his prior albums.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-new_album-97) It was followed later in the year by "[Whisper My Name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whisper_My_Name "Whisper My Name")", his fifteenth number-one on _Billboard_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) The album's [title track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This_Is_Me_(Randy_Travis_song) "This Is Me (Randy Travis song)") and "[The Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Box_(Randy_Travis_song) "The Box (Randy Travis song)")" were both top-ten hits between late 1994 and early 1995 as well.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Travis wrote "The Box" with Buck Moore and later said he became emotional writing and performing the song, as its theme of a father struggling to express love to his children reminded him of his own "fractured" relationship with his father.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019133-102)

Bob Saporiti, then an executive at Warner Bros. Nashville, noted that the failure of _Wind in the Wire_ and length of time since _High Lonesome_ had created "angst" among label executives, but added that they considered _This Is Me_ "back to the basics".[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-new_album-97) To promote the album, Travis hosted an episode of the TNN talk show _Music City Tonight_; the network also re-aired the Country Radio Seminar concert.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-new_album-97) Jurek praised the lyrical contributions of Trey Bruce, [Larry Gatlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Gatlin "Larry Gatlin"), and [Kieran Kane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kieran_Kane "Kieran Kane"), and considered "Whisper My Name" to be "among the greatest songs Travis has ever recorded".[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-103) Nash thought that the lyrics of the singles were among Travis's strongest, also stating that the album had "zippier instrumental touches" than his 1980s albums.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-104) Additionally, Larkin stated that the album was "as strong as ever".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-virgin-11) By mid-1994, _This Is Me_ was certified gold by the RIAA.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-riaa-44) Despite spending most of 1995 without a charted single,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Travis continued to tour throughout the year alongside [Sammy Kershaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Kershaw "Sammy Kershaw") and George Jones.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019135-105)

### 1996–1997: _Full Circle_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 1996–1997: Full Circle")]

[![Image 10: Mark Knopfler playing an electric guitar](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Mar-Knopfler-Pensa-Blue.jpg/250px-Mar-Knopfler-Pensa-Blue.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mar-Knopfler-Pensa-Blue.jpg)

Mark Knopfler wrote Travis's 1996 single "Are We in Trouble Now".

Travis's final album for Warner was _[Full Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full\_Circle\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Full Circle (Randy Travis album)")_ in 1996.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-allmusic-14) Travis told _Billboard_ prior to its release that he and Lehning spent over a year selecting songs for the album because they wanted to be sure they were fully satisfied with its content.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-full_circle-106) Its lead single was "[Are We in Trouble Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Are_We_in_Trouble_Now "Are We in Trouble Now")", a song written by [Mark Knopfler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Knopfler "Mark Knopfler"). Both this song and follow-up "[Would I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Would_I "Would I")" failed to reach the top 20 on the country charts, while neither "Price to Pay" nor a cover of [Roger Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Miller "Roger Miller")'s "[King of the Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_the_Road_(song) "King of the Road (song)")" (which also appeared on the soundtrack of the 1997 movie _[Traveller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traveller\_(1997\_film) "Traveller (1997 film)")_[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-107)) made top 40.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1)_[Richmond Times-Dispatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond\_Times-Dispatch "Richmond Times-Dispatch")_ writer Gordon Ely noted the failure of the album's lead single and questioned whether the album and Travis in general could still be successful in the long term, due to an influx of younger artists in the intervening years.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-gordon-108) Ely considered the album "strong as ever", with a focus on Lehning's production and Travis's voice, as well as the lyrics of "Price to Pay".[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-gordon-108)[Country Standard Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Standard_Time "Country Standard Time") writer Don Yates found the influence of [honky-tonk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honky-tonk "Honky-tonk") in certain songs and praised the lyrics and vocal delivery of "Are We in Trouble Now", but criticized "Would I" as "gimmicky" and closing track "Ants on a Log" as "trite".[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-109) AllMusic writer Thom Owens said of _Full Circle_, "his mid-'90s albums suffered from a tendency to sound a bit too similar to each other. _Full Circle_ solves that problem by simultaneously reaching back into his hardcore honky-tonk roots and moving toward more contemporary material".[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-110)

In mid-1997, Travis announced that he had departed from Warner Bros. due to disagreements over the promotion of _Full Circle_, as well as concerns that the country music industry was beginning to move toward back [country pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_pop "Country pop") influences.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-travels-111) Additionally, Hatcher thought that Warner executives were not allowing her, Travis, and Lehning to have as much liberty on selecting singles as they had on previous albums.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019142-112) At the time of his departure from Warner, Travis was offered contracts by the Nashville divisions of both [Asylum Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asylum_Records "Asylum Records") and the then-new [DreamWorks Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DreamWorks_Records "DreamWorks Records").[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-travels-111) Lehning had just become president of Asylum Records's Nashville division at the time, but Travis chose not to follow him to that label as he did not think Lehning's position was long-term.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019143-113)
