and early 1992, as well as Jackson's number one single "[She's Got the Rhythm (And I Got the Blues)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/She's_Got_the_Rhythm_(And_I_Got_the_Blues) "She's Got the Rhythm (And I Got the Blues)")" later in 1992.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019124-92) Jackson also co-wrote the track "Allergic to the Blues", while Travis wrote "I'm Gonna Have a Little Talk" (featuring backing vocals from gospel group [Take 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take_6 "Take 6")[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-jurek_high-93)) and "Oh, What a Time to Be Me". Travis noted that the project contained more songs written by him than his previous ones did.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-bernard-91) Jurek praised the Jackson co-writes in particular, highlighting their lyrics and vocal deliveries in his review for AllMusic.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-jurek_high-93) Nash also praised the lyrics on the songs co-written by Jackson, while also stating that Travis "never sounded so relaxed or so confident".[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-nash_lonesome-94)

Later the same year, Warner released a pair of [greatest hits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest_hits "Greatest hits") albums: _[Greatest Hits, Volume One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest\_Hits,\_Volume\_One\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Greatest Hits, Volume One (Randy Travis album)")_ and _[Greatest Hits, Volume Two](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest\_Hits,\_Volume\_Two\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Greatest Hits, Volume Two (Randy Travis album)")_. In addition to featuring most of his hit singles to this point, the projects also included four new tracks and the album cut "Reasons I Cheat" from _Storms of Life_.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-beyer-95) Among the new tracks, "[If I Didn't Have You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_I_Didn't_Have_You_(Randy_Travis_song) "If I Didn't Have You (Randy Travis song)")" and "[Look Heart, No Hands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Look_Heart,_No_Hands "Look Heart, No Hands")" both went to number one upon release as singles that year. [Skip Ewing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skip_Ewing "Skip Ewing") and [Max D. Barnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_D._Barnes "Max D. Barnes") wrote the former, while [Trey Bruce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trey_Bruce "Trey Bruce") and [Russell Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Smith_(singer) "Russell Smith (singer)") wrote the latter.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Despite these songs' successes on radio, their follow-up "[An Old Pair of Shoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Old_Pair_of_Shoes "An Old Pair of Shoes")" reached number 21 upon release in early 1993.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Both greatest-hits albums certified platinum in 1995.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-riaa-44)

### 1992–1995: _Wind in the Wire_ and _This Is Me_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 1992–1995: Wind in the Wire and This Is Me")]

Travis took a hiatus from touring in 1992 and 1993, citing exhaustion as the reason for doing so.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019126-96) He and Hatcher chose to spend time at a property in [Maui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui "Maui") they had acquired. According to Travis, the touring hiatus caused some fans and news reporters to believe he had retired,[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-new_album-97) so his publicists issued press releases indicating he was "merely taking a break".[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019127-98) During the hiatus, he released an album of [Western music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_music_(North_America) "Western music (North America)") titled _[Wind in the Wire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind\_in\_the\_Wire "Wind in the Wire")_, a tie-in to a television movie [of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_in_the_Wire_(film) "Wind in the Wire (film)") in which he starred.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) The album was produced by session guitarist Steve Gibson, making it his first since the Randy Ray album not to be produced by Kyle Lehning.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019130-99) It was commercially unsuccessful, with none of its singles reaching top 40 on the _Billboard_ charts.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) However, lead single "[Cowboy Boogie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowboy_Boogie "Cowboy Boogie")" reached number 10 on the Canadian country music charts then published by _[RPM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RPM\_(magazine) "RPM (magazine)")_.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-100) Travis and one of his managers later attributed the album's commercial failure to its [Western swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_swing "Western swing") sound proving unpopular with radio.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-new_album-97)

In late 1993, Travis began working on a follow-up album with Lehning when he was contacted by a representative for the then-under construction [MGM Grand Las Vegas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MGM_Grand_Las_Vegas "MGM Grand Las Vegas") in [Las Vegas, Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Vegas,_Nevada "Las Vegas, Nevada"). The representative wanted Travis to be the first country artist to perform at the new venue once it opened, which inspired Travis to begin touring again. He and Hatcher joined with Jeff Davis, another former manager of Travis's who was then working with [Brother Phelps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brother_Phelps "Brother Phelps"), to assemble a backing band for the Las Vegas shows, which included Lehning as keyboardist.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019131,_132-101) The Las Vegas shows, held in early 1994, were his first concerts in over 14 months.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-new_album-97) Due to the success of these shows, Travis resumed his touring schedule soon afterward. He re-established his existing touring band and performed at a showcase of Warner Bros. artists held in Nashville during the Country Radio Seminar, an annual promotional concert series held by [Country Radio Broadcasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Radio_Broadcasters "Country Radio Broadcasters").[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019131,_132-101)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-new_album-97) At the same time, Travis continued writing and compiling songs for his next studio album. "[Before You Kill Us All](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Before_You_Kill_Us_All "Before You Kill Us All")" was released on February 28, 1994,[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-new_album-97) as the lead single to his next Warner album _[This Is Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This\_Is\_Me\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "This Is Me (Randy Travis album)")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) The song peaked at number two on the _Billboard_ country charts.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Travis and Lehning chose the song because the two wanted "story songs and some with a wink of humor".[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019133-102) Similarly, he told _Billboard_ in 1994 that the song was an example of a more modern and "rowdy" sound he wanted to achieve relative to his prior albums.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-new_album-97) It was followed later in the year by "[Whisper My Name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whisper_My_Name "Whisper My Name")", his fifteenth number-one on _Billboard_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) The album's [title track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This_Is_Me_(Randy_Travis_song) "This Is Me (Randy Travis song)") and "[The Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Box_(Randy_Travis_song) "The Box (Randy Travis song)")" were both top-ten hits between late 1994 and early 1995 as well.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Travis wrote "The Box" with Buck Moore and later said he became emotional writing and performing the song, as its theme of a father struggling to express love to his children reminded him of his own "fractured" relationship with his father.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019133-102)

Bob Saporiti, then an executive at Warner Bros. Nashville, noted that the failure of _Wind in the Wire_ and length of time since _High Lonesome_ had created "angst" among label executives, but added that they considered _This Is Me_ "back to the basics".[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-new_album-97) To promote the album, Travis hosted an episode of the TNN talk show _Music City Tonight_; the network also re-aired the Country Radio Seminar concert.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-new_album-97) Jurek praised the lyrical contributions of Trey Bruce, [Larry Gatlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Gatlin "Larry Gatlin"), and [Kieran Kane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kieran_Kane "Kieran Kane"), and considered "Whisper My Name" to be "among the greatest songs Travis has ever recorded".[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-103) Nash thought that the lyrics of the singles were among Travis's strongest, also stating that the album had "zippier instrumental touches" than his 1980s albums.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-104) Additionally, Larkin stated that the album was "as strong as ever".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-virgin-11) By mid-1994, _This Is Me_ was certified gold by the RIAA.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-riaa-44) Despite spending most of 1995 without a charted single,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Travis continued to tour throughout the year alongside [Sammy Kershaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Kershaw "Sammy Kershaw") and George Jones.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019135-105)

### 1996–1997: _Full Circle_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 1996–1997: Full Circle")]

[![Image 10: Mark Knopfler playing an electric guitar](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Mar-Knopfler-Pensa-Blue.jpg/250px-Mar-Knopfler-Pensa-Blue.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mar-Knopfler-Pensa-Blue.jpg)

Mark Knopfler wrote Travis's 1996 single "Are We in Trouble Now".

Travis's final album for Warner was _[Full Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full\_Circle\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Full Circle (Randy Travis album)")_ in 1996.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) Travis told _Billboard_ prior to its release that he and Lehning spent over a year selecting songs for the album because they wanted to be sure they were fully satisfied with its content.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-full_circle-106) Its lead single was "[Are We in Trouble Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Are_We_in_Trouble_Now "Are We in Trouble Now")", a song written by [Mark Knopfler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Knopfler "Mark Knopfler"). Both this song and follow-up "[Would I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Would_I "Would I")" failed to reach the top 20 on the country charts, while neither "Price to Pay" nor a cover of [Roger Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Miller "Roger Miller")'s "[King of the Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_the_Road_(song) "King of the Road (song)")" (which also appeared on the soundtrack of the 1997 movie _[Traveller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traveller\_(1997\_film) "Traveller (1997 film)")_[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-107)) made top 40.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1)_[Richmond Times-Dispatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond\_Times-Dispatch "Richmond Times-Dispatch")_ writer Gordon Ely noted the failure of the album's lead single and questioned whether the album and Travis in general could still be successful in the long term, due to an influx of younger artists in the intervening years.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-gordon-108) Ely considered the album "strong as ever", with a focus on Lehning's production and Travis's voice, as well as the lyrics of "Price to Pay".[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-gordon-108)[Country Standard Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Standard_Time "Country Standard Time") writer Don Yates found the influence of [honky-tonk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honky-tonk "Honky-tonk") in certain songs and praised the lyrics and vocal delivery of "Are We in Trouble Now", but criticized "Would I" as "gimmicky" and closing track "Ants on a Log" as "trite".[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-109) AllMusic writer Thom Owens said of _Full Circle_, "his mid-'90s albums suffered from a tendency to sound a bit too similar to each other. _Full Circle_ solves that problem by simultaneously reaching back into his hardcore honky-tonk roots and moving toward more contemporary material".[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-110)

In mid-1997, Travis announced that he had departed from Warner Bros. due to disagreements over the promotion of _Full Circle_, as well as concerns that the country music industry was beginning to move toward back [country pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_pop "Country pop") influences.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-travels-111) Additionally, Hatcher thought that Warner executives were not allowing her, Travis, and Lehning to have as much liberty on selecting singles as they had on previous albums.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019142-112) At the time of his departure from Warner, Travis was offered contracts by the Nashville divisions of both [Asylum Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asylum_Records "Asylum Records") and the then-new [DreamWorks Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DreamWorks_Records "DreamWorks Records").[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-travels-111) Lehning had just become president of Asylum Records's Nashville division at the time, but Travis chose not to follow him to that label as he did not think Lehning's position was long-term.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019143-113)

### 1997–1999: DreamWorks Records

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 1997–1999: DreamWorks Records")]

By August 1997, Travis had become the first artist signed to DreamWorks Records's Nashville division.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-114) The new label's president was musician and producer James Stroud, who had played on some of Travis' singles, including "Forever and Ever, Amen".[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019135,_136,_142-115) As Lehning's duties at Asylum left him temporarily unavailable, Stroud and [Byron Gallimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byron_Gallimore "Byron Gallimore") produced Travis for DreamWorks.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019143-113) "[Out of My Bones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_My_Bones "Out of My Bones")" was the first single release for DreamWorks Nashville, in 1997.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-116) Co-written by [Gary Burr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Burr "Gary Burr") and [Sharon Vaughn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharon_Vaughn "Sharon Vaughn"), it peaked at number two on the country charts early in 1998.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) It appeared on his first DreamWorks album _[You and You Alone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You\_and\_You\_Alone\_(album) "You and You Alone (album)")_, issued in April.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) The project also accounted for the top-ten hits "[The Hole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hole_(song) "The Hole (song)")" and "[Spirit of a Boy, Wisdom of a Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_of_a_Boy,_Wisdom_of_a_Man "Spirit of a Boy, Wisdom of a Man")" and the top-20 "[Stranger in My Mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stranger_in_My_Mirror "Stranger in My Mirror")". Both "The Hole" and "Stranger in My Mirror" were co-written by Skip Ewing.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) "Spirit of a Boy, Wisdom of a Man" was previously recorded by [Mark Collie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Collie "Mark Collie") on his 1995 album _[Tennessee Plates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee\_Plates "Tennessee Plates")_.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-117) Jeffrey B. Remz of Country Standard Time criticized the heavy drums on "I Did My Part", but otherwise praised the use of acoustic instruments and the strength of Travis's voice.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-remz_alone-118)_[Lincoln Journal Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln\_Journal\_Star "Lincoln Journal Star")_ writer L. Kent Wolgamott noted the presence of [fiddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiddle "Fiddle") and [steel guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel_guitar "Steel guitar") in the production while also calling Travis's voice "expressive".[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-lincoln-119)

In 1999, Travis was one of several artists on the collaborative song "Same Old Train", featured on the multi-artist album _[Tribute to Tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribute\_to\_Tradition "Tribute to Tradition")_. Other acts appearing on the song included [Clint Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clint_Black "Clint Black"), [Dwight Yoakam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_Yoakam "Dwight Yoakam"), and [Pam Tillis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pam_Tillis "Pam Tillis"), along with [Marty Stuart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Stuart "Marty Stuart"), who wrote and produced it.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-120) The track won a [Grammy Award for Best Country Collaboration with Vocals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Country_Collaboration_with_Vocals "Grammy Award for Best Country Collaboration with Vocals").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-grammy-54) Travis's second and final DreamWorks album _[A Man Ain't Made of Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Man\_Ain't\_Made\_of\_Stone "A Man Ain't Made of Stone")_ released in 1999.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14)[The title track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Man_Ain't_Made_of_Stone_(song) "A Man Ain't Made of Stone (song)") (co-written by Burr) was a top-20 country hit by year's end, but the other singles, "Where Can I Surrender", "A Little Left of Center", and "I'll Be Right Here Loving You", all missed the top 40.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Gallimore and Stroud recorded the album largely in [Santa Fe, New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Fe,_New_Mexico "Santa Fe, New Mexico"), where Travis and Hatcher had a house at the time.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-121) Following the failure of the later singles, Travis exited DreamWorks in 2000.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-122) Shortly after his departure, Travis told Country Standard Time that he chose to leave DreamWorks because he felt the label had not properly distributed the album. He added that Stroud's production style put too much emphasis on instrumentation instead of his singing voice.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-inspiration-123)

### 2000–2003: Switch to gospel and "Three Wooden Crosses"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 2000–2003: Switch to gospel and \"Three Wooden Crosses\"")]

[![Image 11: Kenny Chesney, singing with one arm extended and the other holding a microphone](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Kenny_Chesney_20070830.jpg/250px-Kenny_Chesney_20070830.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kenny_Chesney_20070830.jpg)

Kenny Chesney (pictured in 2007) collaborated with Travis on the 2000 single "Baptism".

While he was still on Warner, Travis had begun working with Lehning on a [gospel music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music") album.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-inspirational_allmusic-124)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-125) Other than a cover of "[Amazing Grace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazing_Grace "Amazing Grace")", the two intentionally sought to include original content. Travis finished the tracks at a time when he was not on a record label. Through a connection Lehning had with [Word Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_Records "Word Records") executive Barry Landis, Travis was signed to that label in late 2000 and released the gospel album, by then titled _[Inspirational Journey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inspirational\_Journey "Inspirational Journey")_.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019149,_150-126)[Waylon Jennings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waylon_Jennings "Waylon Jennings") and [Jessi Colter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessi_Colter "Jessi Colter") provided guest vocals on "The Carpenter".[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-inspirational_allmusic-124)[Kenny Chesney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Chesney "Kenny Chesney") sang duet vocals on "[Baptism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptism_(Kenny_Chesney_and_Randy_Travis_song) "Baptism (Kenny Chesney and Randy Travis song)")" (also titled "Down with the Old Man (Up with the New)"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-127) which served as the first single. The two had previously recorded the song for Chesney's 1999 album _[Everywhere We Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everywhere\_We\_Go "Everywhere We Go")_.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-inspiration-123)_Inspirational Journey_ won two [Dove Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dove_Awards "Dove Awards") in 2001: Bluegrass Album of the Year for the album itself, and Country Recorded Song of the Year for "Baptism".[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-dove-128) AllMusic reviewer Todd Everett found influences of bluegrass, [Don Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Williams "Don Williams"), and Lefty Frizzell, and found it consistent with Travis's 1980s and 1990s albums in tone.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-inspirational_allmusic-124) Alanna Nash of _Entertainment Weekly_ was less favorable, as she thought that the album had strong opening tracks but added that "midway, it deteriorates into Nashville formula, with simplistic homilies [and] overblown production".[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-129)

Following the [September 11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks") in 2001, Travis co-wrote and released a promotional patriotic single titled "America Will Always Stand".[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-130) Proceeds from sales of the single were donated to the [American Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Red_Cross "American Red Cross").[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-131) He continued with Word as a gospel artist and put out his next album for the label, _[Rise and Shine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rise\_and\_Shine\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Rise and Shine (Randy Travis album)")_, in 2002. The lead single was "[Three Wooden Crosses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Wooden_Crosses "Three Wooden Crosses")". According to Travis, songwriters [Kim Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Williams_(songwriter) "Kim Williams (songwriter)") and [Doug Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doug_Johnson_(record_producer) "Doug Johnson (record producer)") had pitched the song to [Michael Peterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Peterson_(singer) "Michael Peterson (singer)"), who at the time was recording with Lehning. Peterson suggested Lehning take the song to Travis, for whom he thought it was better suited.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019152,_153-132) By early 2003, "Three Wooden Crosses" became Travis's sixteenth and final number-one on _Billboard_ Hot Country Songs. It also accounted for his highest solo peak on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") at number 31. The project charted one other single in "Pray for the Fish", which fell below top 40 on the country charts.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Robert L. Doerschuk of AllMusic called the album "a strong performance, presented with flawless studio clarity and persuasive, understated feeling."[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-robert-133) Remz noted the consistency of Lehning's production and Travis's voice, as well as the presence of original songs co-written by Travis.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-134) In October 2003, _Rise and Shine_ was certified gold.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-riaa-44) At the 2004 Grammy Awards, _Rise and Shine_ won a [Grammy Award for Best Southern, Country or Bluegrass Gospel Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Southern,_Country_or_Bluegrass_Gospel_Album "Grammy Award for Best Southern, Country or Bluegrass Gospel Album"), while "Three Wooden Crosses" was nominated for Best Male Country Vocal Performance.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-grammy-54) That same year, "Pray for the Fish" won a Dove Award for Country Recorded Song of the Year.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-dove-128)

### 2003–2007: Continued gospel albums

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 2003–2007: Continued gospel albums")]

His next gospel album was 2003's _[Worship & Faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worship\_&\_Faith "Worship & Faith")_. Unlike the previous projects, it included 20 acoustic covers of existing praise songs and hymns.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-135) Among the tracks included were "[In the Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_the_Garden_(1912_song) "In the Garden (1912 song)")", "[How Great Thou Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How_Great_Thou_Art "How Great Thou Art")", "[Peace in the Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_in_the_Valley "Peace in the Valley")", and "[I'll Fly Away](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'll_Fly_Away "I'll Fly Away")". Jurek called the album "direct, unfiltered, hard-line gospel at its best, by a master" in a review for AllMusic.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-136)_Worship & Faith_ also became a gold album,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-riaa-44) and accounted for his second consecutive Grammy Award for Best Southern, Country or Bluegrass Gospel Album.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-grammy-54) A year later he released _[Passing Through](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passing\_Through\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Passing Through (Randy Travis album)")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) This album accounted for his last solo chart singles until 2024, "Four Walls" and "Angels".[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019152,_153-132) The latter was Travis's 50th entry on the chart.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Co-writers on the album included [Jamie O'Hara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamie_O'Hara_(singer) "Jamie O'Hara (singer)"), Dennis Linde, Sharon Vaughn, and Travis.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-passing-137) "Four Walls" was previously cut by [Keith Harling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Harling "Keith Harling"),[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-138) while the album track "That Was Us" was previously recorded by both [Tracy Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracy_Lawrence "Tracy Lawrence") and [Chad Brock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chad_Brock "Chad Brock"), whose version was a single in 2003.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-139)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-passing-137)[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn201753-140) Erlewine wrote of _Passing Through_, "It's inspirational music in the purest sense—it doesn't preach, it instructs and inspires through its carefully observed tales."[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-passing-137) Travis received a star on the [Hollywood Walk of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_Walk_of_Fame "Hollywood Walk of Fame") in September 2004.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-141)

In 2005, Travis released another gospel album, _[Glory Train: Songs of Faith, Worship, and Praise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glory\_Train:\_Songs\_of\_Faith,\_Worship,\_and\_Praise "Glory Train: Songs of Faith, Worship, and Praise")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) It, too, won a Grammy Award for Best Southern, Country or Bluegrass Gospel Album.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-grammy-54) Some tracks on the project included backing vocals from [the Blind Boys of Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blind_Boys_of_Alabama "The Blind Boys of Alabama"). Unlike the previous albums, it contained a mix of Black spirituals and [contemporary Christian music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Christian_music "Contemporary Christian music") such as [Darlene Zschech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darlene_Zschech "Darlene Zschech")'s "[Shout to the Lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shout_to_the_Lord "Shout to the Lord")". Erlewine thought the inclusion of such material made it "Travis's best gospel album to date".[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-142) Writing for _[The Atlanta Journal-Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Atlanta\_Journal-Constitution "The Atlanta Journal-Constitution")_, Nick Marino praised Travis's "[bluesy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues")" vocals and the variety of songs.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-143) Altogether, Travis's first four gospel albums each won the Dove Award for Country Album of the Year, accounting for a streak of four consecutive wins in that category from 2003 to 2006.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-dove-128) Also in 2006, Travis began recording footage for a Christmas DVD titled _Christmas on the Pecos_. This footage consisted of him singing Christmas songs and reading [Helen Steiner Rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Steiner_Rice "Helen Steiner Rice")'s poem "The Christmas Guest" inside the Big Room, a cavern at [Carlsbad Caverns National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlsbad_Caverns_National_Park "Carlsbad Caverns National Park").[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019160,_161-144)[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-145) Some of the performances also included vocal accompaniment from the choir of the Carlsbad First Baptist Church. The DVD was released in late 2006.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019160,_161-144) Another Christmas project, the album _[Songs of the Season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songs\_of\_the\_Season "Songs of the Season")_, followed in 2007.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-146)

### 2008–2011: Return to Warner and Carrie Underwood version of "I Told You So"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 2008–2011: Return to Warner and Carrie Underwood version of \"I Told You So\"")]

In 2008, he released his next studio album _[Around the Bend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Around\_the\_Bend\_(album) "Around the Bend (album)")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) The project was his first country music release since _A Man Ain't Made of Stone_.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019165-147)[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-jeff-148) The album also placed him back on Warner, which had been a distributor of his Word Records releases.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-149) Travis promoted the album in an interview with [WSM-FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSM-FM "WSM-FM") radio host [Bill Cody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Cody_(radio_host) "Bill Cody (radio host)").[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019165-147) He also released its lead single "Faith in You" as a free download from his website.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-150) "Dig Two Graves" was the project's second single.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-jeff-148) In addition to these songs, the album included a cover of [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan")'s "[Don't Think Twice, It's All Right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Think_Twice,_It's_All_Right "Don't Think Twice, It's All Right")".[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019165-147) Jeff DeDekker of _[The Leader-Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Leader-Post "The Leader-Post")_ noted that while it was not marketed as a Christian album, individual songs still held themes of "redemption and the afterlife".[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-jeff-148) He praised the lyrics of "Dig Two Graves" and Travis's singing voice in particular.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-jeff-148) Erlewine criticized the use of a [string section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_section "String section") on "Faith in You", but otherwise reviewed the album's song selection and Travis's voice with favor.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-bend-151) Despite not being explicitly marketed as a Christian album, it won Travis his eighth and final Dove Award, in the category of Country Album of the Year.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-dove-128)

[![Image 12: A bust shot of Carrie Underwood in a purple dress](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/191125_Carrie_Underwood_at_the_2019_American_Music_Awards.png/250px-191125_Carrie_Underwood_at_the_2019_American_Music_Awards.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:191125_Carrie_Underwood_at_the_2019_American_Music_Awards.png)

Carrie Underwood had a hit in 2009 with a rendition of Travis's "I Told You So".

[Carrie Underwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrie_Underwood "Carrie Underwood") recorded a cover of "I Told You So" on her late-2007 album _[Carnival Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnival\_Ride "Carnival Ride")_.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-152) Her version was released in January 2009 as the album's fifth single. Two months after her rendition was released to radio, disc jockey Jesse Tack at [WUBE-FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WUBE-FM "WUBE-FM") in [Cincinnati, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati,_Ohio "Cincinnati, Ohio") combined Underwood's recording with the vocal track from Travis's original and distributed the results to 75 other radio stations. Due to the popularity of the combined recording with radio listeners, Underwood and Travis performed the song together on _[American Idol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Idol "American Idol")_ soon after.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-153) The two also recorded an official duet version, which was sent to radio as well.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-154) With both Travis and Underwood receiving chart credit, the duet version of "I Told You So" peaked at number two on the country charts in 2009, and accounted for Travis's highest overall _Billboard_ Hot 100 peak of number nine.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366,_374,_375-155) The duet won both artists the 2010 Grammy Award for Best Country Collaboration with Vocals.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-grammy-54)

Travis continued to record for Warner at the time. To honor the 25th anniversary of _Storms of Life_, he released _[Anniversary Celebration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anniversary\_Celebration "Anniversary Celebration")_ in 2011.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) The album consisted entirely of collaborations, on both re-recordings of Travis's previous singles and new songs.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-156) Among the artists involved were [Zac Brown Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zac_Brown_Band "Zac Brown Band") ("Forever and Ever, Amen"), Kenny Chesney ("He Walked on Water"), and [Jamey Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamey_Johnson "Jamey Johnson") ("A Few Ole Country Boys"). Alan Jackson contributed to a medley of Travis's "Better Class of Losers" and Jackson's "She's Got the Rhythm (And I Got the Blues)", both of which the two co-wrote. George Jones, [Lorrie Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorrie_Morgan "Lorrie Morgan"), [Ray Price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Price "Ray Price"), [Connie Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connie_Smith "Connie Smith"), [Joe Stampley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Stampley "Joe Stampley"), and [Gene Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Watson "Gene Watson") all provided vocals to the track "Didn't We Shine". Karlie Justus of Country Standard Time highlighted these tracks in particular among the strongest.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-justus-157)

### 2013–2018: Stroke and subsequent career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: 2013–2018: Stroke and subsequent career")]

In July 2013, Travis experienced difficulty breathing while working out at his home gym.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-damaged-158) He was hospitalized in [Dallas, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas,_Texas "Dallas, Texas"), for [viral cardiomyopathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viral_cardiomyopathy "Viral cardiomyopathy"). While undergoing treatment, Travis suffered [congestive heart failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congestive_heart_failure "Congestive heart failure") and a [stroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stroke "Stroke").[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-159)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-160)[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-rauf-161) The stroke affected the left side of Travis's brain, impacting movement on the right side of his body. Travis was placed on [life support](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_support "Life support") after the infection caused his lungs to collapse, and was declared to have a one percent chance of survival.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-rauf-161) The infection, subsequent stroke, and three separate bouts of [pneumonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia "Pneumonia") led to Travis undergoing three [tracheostomies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracheostomy "Tracheostomy") and two brain surgeries.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-rauf-161) He also suffered [aphasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphasia "Aphasia"), lost the ability to speak and sing, and had vision problems. These issues were mitigated through years of therapy.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-rauf-161) While the stroke largely left him unable to sing or speak, he soon began recovering. According to [Taste of Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taste_of_Country "Taste of Country"), within a year of the stroke, he was able to walk short distances without assistance, and was re-learning to write and to play guitar.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-162)

Despite his stroke, Travis released a pair of previously recorded [cover song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_song "Cover song") projects between late 2013 and early 2014. The first was _[Influence Vol. 1: The Man I Am](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Influence\_Vol.\_1:\_The\_Man\_I\_Am "Influence Vol. 1: The Man I Am")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) Among the covers were Lefty Frizzell's "[Saginaw, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saginaw,_Michigan_(song) "Saginaw, Michigan (song)")", [Ernest Tubb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Tubb "Ernest Tubb")'s "Thanks a Lot", and George Jones's "[Why Baby Why](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Why_Baby_Why "Why Baby Why")". The only track on the album not to be a cover was "Tonight I'm Playin' Possum", a duet with [Joe Nichols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Nichols "Joe Nichols"). Remz noted that many of the cover songs chosen had previously been written or performed by [Merle Haggard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merle_Haggard "Merle Haggard"), and spoke favorably of Lehning's "low-key" production.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-163) The second volume of this project, _[Influence Vol. 2: The Man I Am](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Influence\_Vol.\_2:\_The\_Man\_I\_Am "Influence Vol. 2: The Man I Am")_, followed in 2014.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14)[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-mayhem-164) Like the first volume, it included covers of Haggard, Tubb, and Frizzell, as well as [Kris Kristofferson](https:/

**Randy Bruce Traywick** (born May 4, 1959), known professionally as **Randy Travis**, is an American [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") and [gospel music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music") singer and songwriter, as well as a film and television actor. Active since 1979, he has recorded over 20 studio albums and charted more than 50 singles on _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard\_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")_'s [Hot Country Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Country_Songs "Hot Country Songs") charts, including sixteen that reached the number-one position.

Travis's commercial success began in the mid-1980s with the release of his album _[Storms of Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storms\_of\_Life "Storms of Life")_, which was certified triple-platinum by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America"). He followed up his major-label debut with a string of platinum and multi-platinum albums, but his commercial success declined throughout the 1990s. In 1997, he left [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Records "Warner Bros. Records") for [DreamWorks Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DreamWorks_Records "DreamWorks Records"); he signed to [Word Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_Records "Word Records") for a series of gospel albums beginning in 2000 before transferring back to Warner at the end of the 21st century's first decade. His musical accolades include seven [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards"), eleven [ACM Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Country_Music "Academy of Country Music"), eight [Dove Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dove_Awards "Dove Awards"), a star on the [Hollywood Walk of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_Walk_of_Fame "Hollywood Walk of Fame"), and a 2016 induction into the [Country Music Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Music_Hall_of_Fame "Country Music Hall of Fame"). Major songs of his include "[On the Other Hand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Other_Hand "On the Other Hand")", "[Forever and Ever, Amen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forever_and_Ever,_Amen "Forever and Ever, Amen")", "[I Told You So](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Told_You_So_(Randy_Travis_song) "I Told You So (Randy Travis song)")", "[Hard Rock Bottom of Your Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_Rock_Bottom_of_Your_Heart "Hard Rock Bottom of Your Heart")", and "[Three Wooden Crosses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Wooden_Crosses "Three Wooden Crosses")".

He is noted as a key figure in the [neotraditional country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neotraditional_country "Neotraditional country") movement, a return to more traditional sounds within the genre following the [country pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_pop "Country pop") crossovers of the early 1980s. Nearly all of his albums were produced or co-produced by [Kyle Lehning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyle_Lehning "Kyle Lehning"), and feature frequent co-writing credits from [Paul Overstreet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Overstreet "Paul Overstreet"), [Don Schlitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Schlitz "Don Schlitz"), and [Skip Ewing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skip_Ewing "Skip Ewing"). Critics have compared his [baritone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baritone "Baritone") singing voice to other artists such as [Lefty Frizzell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lefty_Frizzell "Lefty Frizzell"), [Merle Haggard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merle_Haggard "Merle Haggard"), and [George Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Jones "George Jones"). Since surviving a near-fatal [stroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stroke "Stroke") in 2013, which severely limited his singing and speaking ability, he has released archival recordings and made limited public appearances. James Dupré has toured singing Travis's songs with his road band. Between mid-2024 and January 2025, Travis released two new songs where his voice was re-created via [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence").

Travis's acting career includes roles in the television movies _[Wind in the Wire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind\_in\_the\_Wire\_(film) "Wind in the Wire (film)")_ (1993) and _[A Holiday to Remember](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Holiday\_to\_Remember "A Holiday to Remember")_ (1995), as well as the [Patrick Swayze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Swayze "Patrick Swayze") movie _[Black Dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black\_Dog\_(1998\_film) "Black Dog (1998 film)")_ (1998).

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Randy Bruce Traywick was born May 4, 1959, in [Marshville, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshville,_North_Carolina "Marshville, North Carolina").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) He is the second of six children to Bobbie and Harold Traywick.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic19901%E2%80%933,_8,_9-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham20193,_4-3) Harold Traywick worked as a meat packer and also built houses.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic19908,_9-4) He also enjoyed listening to [country music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") such as [Ernest Tubb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Tubb "Ernest Tubb") and [Patsy Cline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsy_Cline "Patsy Cline"), in addition to singing, playing guitar, and writing his own songs. By the time Randy was eight years old, his father sent him and his brothers, Ricky and David, to the house of a friend named Kate Magnum, who taught them how to play guitar.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199012-5) Harold also constructed a stage behind the family house, where he invited friends over to hear his sons sing.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199013-6) Randy and Ricky performed publicly for the first time in 1968 at a talent show held at the local [elementary school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elementary_school "Elementary school"); while the brothers did not win, they continued to perform at local talent shows, with David later joining to accompany them on [bass guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_guitar "Bass guitar").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199013,_14-7)

Randy dropped out of school in the ninth grade.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199018-8) As a teenager, he committed a number of crimes, including [reckless driving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reckless_driving "Reckless driving") after he crashed Ricky's car in a cornfield, breaking into a church to hold a party, [driving under the influence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Driving_under_the_influence "Driving under the influence"), [resisting arrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resisting_arrest "Resisting arrest"), and stealing knives and watches from a local store.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199018-8) On his seventeenth birthday, Randy was arrested for [public intoxication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_intoxication "Public intoxication") and faced imprisonment.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199019-9) Despite his charges, [Don Cusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cusic "Don Cusic") noted in the 1990 book _Randy Travis: The King of the New Country Traditionalists_ that his parents still supported him, as they paid his [bail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bail "Bail") and appeared in court whenever he was arrested.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199019-9)

In 1977, the Traywicks entered a talent competition held in [Charlotte, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte,_North_Carolina "Charlotte, North Carolina"), after hearing an advertisement for it on the radio. The grand prize for the contest was $100 cash and a recording session.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199021-10) The contest consisted of eight semi-final audition rounds held every Tuesday at Country City USA, a [nightclub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nightclub "Nightclub") co-owned by Randy's future wife, Mary Elizabeth "Lib" Hatcher.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199021-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-virgin-11) At the performance, Randy played [rhythm guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_guitar "Rhythm guitar") and sang, while Ricky played [lead guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_guitar "Lead guitar"). However, Ricky had to drop out of the competition partway through because he had to serve time at a [youth detention center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth_detention_center "Youth detention center"), leaving Randy to continue as a solo act. Randy ended up winning the competition.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199021,_22-12) Afterward, he talked with Hatcher about his then-impending arrest charges for [hot-wiring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot-wiring "Hot-wiring") a neighbor's truck.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199022-13) Hatcher and disc jockey John Harper, who also worked at the club, chose to represent Randy in court, which led to him serving [probation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probation "Probation") and coming under the custody of Hatcher in lieu of a jail sentence.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199022-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) Additionally, Hatcher employed Randy as a singer at Country City USA.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199022-13) During this time, Hatcher advised him on his singing and performance. Harold would attend Randy's performances in this timespan, but was later banned from the club after altercations with patrons.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199027,_28-15)

## Music career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Music career")]

### 1979–1984: Beginnings and initial singles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1979–1984: Beginnings and initial singles")]

Hatcher booked a number of country music singers to perform at her club as a means of making connections with country music personnel in [Nashville, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee "Nashville, Tennessee").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199029,_30-16) One such singer, [Joe Stampley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Stampley "Joe Stampley"), agreed to produce a session for Traywick in Nashville. Hatcher paid $10,000 for the recording session and promotion, which was done through an independent label based out of [Shreveport, Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shreveport,_Louisiana "Shreveport, Louisiana"), called [Paula Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewel_Records_(Shreveport_record_label) "Jewel Records (Shreveport record label)"). The session accounted for the singles "She's My Woman" and "I'll Take Any Willing Woman". Traywick and Hatcher promoted copies of the single to radio stations throughout the [Southern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States "Southern United States") in 1979. The former reached number 91 on _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard\_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")_'s [Hot Country Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Country_Songs "Hot Country Songs") charts.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199030-17) After the failure of these singles, Hatcher and Traywick continued submitting [demo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demo_(music) "Demo (music)") recordings to executives but were unable to garner interest at first.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199031-18) In 1981, Traywick and Hatcher chose to move to Nashville to put themselves closer to the center of the country music industry. Despite this, they would still travel back to Charlotte on weekends to tend to business at Country City USA, which by that point had relocated to a larger building.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199029,_40-19) They supported themselves by renting out part of their Nashville house to songwriter and producer [Keith Stegall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Stegall "Keith Stegall"), who used it as an office.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199039,_41-20) Stegall then introduced the two to song publisher and disc jockey [Charlie Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Monk_(broadcaster) "Charlie Monk (broadcaster)") at a golf game, which led to Traywick performing songs for Monk. Stegall also submitted Traywick's demos to various Nashville producers to garner interest in a recording contract. Traywick recorded one session with producer John Ragsdale for the intent of signing him to [Curb Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curb_Records "Curb Records"), but the label ultimately chose not to sign him.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199042,_43-21)

In 1982 Hatcher began managing a nightclub called the Nashville Palace through the recommendation of singer [Ray Pillow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Pillow "Ray Pillow"). She initially hired Traywick to wash dishes, but soon began to have him perform there as well. By this point, he began crediting himself as Randy Ray, as he and Hatcher thought the name was easier to pronounce than "Traywick".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199046,_47-22) Hatcher also rented her in-house office space out to other industry executives, including staff of _[Radio & Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio\_&\_Records "Radio & Records")_ magazine; meanwhile, Randy Ray continued to work on his songwriting under Stegall's mentorship.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199051,_52-23) By the end of the year, Hatcher and Nashville Palace owner John Hobbs financed an independent album titled _Randy Ray Live at the Nashville Palace_, which consisted of ten songs recorded by him at the Palace. Stegall served as producer on this project.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199055%E2%80%9357-24) He also auditioned on _You Can Be a Star_, a talent show on the former [TNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TNN_(American_TV_channel) "TNN (American TV channel)"), in early 1983 and placed second behind Lang Scott, who would later marry country singer [Linda Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Davis "Linda Davis").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199054-25)[Ralph Emery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Emery "Ralph Emery") also invited him to perform several times on the TNN talk show _[Nashville Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville\_Now "Nashville Now")_, which he hosted.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199063,_64-26)

Despite the exposure from _Nashville Now_, he still failed to secure a recording contract throughout 1984.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199063,_64-26) Martha Sharp, then working in [artists and repertoire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artists_and_repertoire "Artists and repertoire") (A&R) at [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Records "Warner Bros. Records")'s Nashville division, attended a seminar in late 1984 where executives suggested signing attractive young artists with a "traditional" sound. Through mutual contacts with Monk and Stegall, she became aware of Randy Ray, who at the time was working on more songs with the latter.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199072-27) Sharp arranged for him to be signed to a contract initially consisting of four songs. Executives disliked the name "Randy Ray" as they thought it sounded "[podunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podunk "Podunk")", and Sharp suggested "Randy Travis".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199072,_73-28)

### 1985–1986: _Storms of Life_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1985–1986: Storms of Life")]

Travis signed with Warner Nashville in early 1985. His first contract with them resulted in the recording of four songs: "Prairie Rose", "[On the Other Hand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Other_Hand "On the Other Hand")", "Carrying Fire", and "Reasons I Cheat". "Prairie Rose" appeared on the soundtrack of the 1985 film _[Rustlers' Rhapsody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustlers'\_Rhapsody "Rustlers' Rhapsody")_.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199074%E2%80%9375-29)[Keith Whitley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Whitley "Keith Whitley") also recorded "On the Other Hand" for his 1985 debut album _[L.A. to Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L.A.\_to\_Miami "L.A. to Miami")_.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-30) These four songs were all recorded in the same session, with Stegall and [Kyle Lehning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyle_Lehning "Kyle Lehning") co-producing. At the time, Lehning was best known for producing [Dan Seals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Seals "Dan Seals") and had also worked with Stegall on his own singles for [Epic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_Records "Epic Records"). Although Lehning did not want to work with Travis at first, he chose to do so after Monk and Sharp encouraged him.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199074,_75-31) After recording these songs, Travis appeared on _Nashville Now_ again on May 17, 1985, where he performed with [Johnny Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Russell_(singer) "Johnny Russell (singer)") and [Lorrie Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorrie_Morgan "Lorrie Morgan").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199077-32) Warner also included him among the performers at their talent showcase at the Fan Fair (now [CMA Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CMA_Music_Festival "CMA Music Festival")) in downtown Nashville in mid-1985.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199080,_81-33) Warner released "On the Other Hand" on July 29, 1985,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-lawrence-34) and it peaked at number 67 on the _Billboard_ country charts.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199081-35) The follow-up "[1982](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_(Randy_Travis_song) "1982 (Randy Travis song)")" peaked at number six on the country charts in early 1986,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) thus becoming Travis's first hit single.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199082%E2%80%9383-36) Following the success of "1982", Travis was booked as an opening act for [Barbara Mandrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Mandrell "Barbara Mandrell") and [T. G. Sheppard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._G._Sheppard "T. G. Sheppard"), leading to both Travis and Hatcher quitting the Palace.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199083%E2%80%9385-37) The song's success also led to him performing on the [Grand Ole Opry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Ole_Opry "Grand Ole Opry") for the first time in March 1986.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199086-38) He also received an award for Top New Male Vocalist from the [Academy of Country Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Country_Music "Academy of Country Music") (ACM).[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-acm-39) This was followed by further opening act gigs throughout early 1986, which resulted in gigs from [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") to [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"). Hatcher and Travis bought a former [bread truck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-stop_truck "Multi-stop truck") which they converted to a [tour bus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_bus "Tour bus"), in addition to hiring a five-piece band to perform with him.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199093-40)

[![Image 6: A head shot of singer-songwriter Don Schlitz](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Don_Schlitz%2C_January_2024.jpg/250px-Don_Schlitz%2C_January_2024.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Don_Schlitz,_January_2024.jpg)

Don Schlitz co-wrote Travis's singles "On the Other Hand", "Forever and Ever, Amen", and "Deeper Than the Holler".

After "1982" became Travis's first top-ten hit, Warner executives chose to re-release "On the Other Hand". Nick Hunter, who promoted singles to country radio for Warner, noted that the song was popular in sales and listener demand despite its initially low chart peak.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199097-41) Upon re-release, "On the Other Hand" became his first number-one single on the _Billboard_ country charts in July 1986.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199097%E2%80%9399-42) "On the Other Hand" and "1982" were both included on Travis's debut album for Warner, _[Storms of Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storms\_of\_Life "Storms of Life")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) The album was released on June 2, 1986, and sold over 100,000 copies in its first sales week in addition to reaching number one on [Top Country Albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_Country_Albums "Top Country Albums").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199098-43) Six years after its release, the album was [certified triple platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_certification "Music recording certification") by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") (RIAA), honoring U.S. sales of three million copies.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-riaa-44) One of the tracks, Travis's own composition "Send My Body", had previously appeared on the Randy Ray album in 1982.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199099-45) Lehning and Stegall co-produced the album; they also contributed on keyboard and guitar, respectively. Other musicians on the project included drummers [Eddie Bayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Bayers "Eddie Bayers"), [Larrie Londin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larrie_Londin "Larrie Londin"), and [James Stroud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Stroud "James Stroud"); guitarist [Larry Byrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Byrom "Larry Byrom"); [Dobro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobro "Dobro") player [Jerry Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Douglas "Jerry Douglas"); bassist [David Hungate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hungate "David Hungate"); and backing vocals from Lehning, [Baillie & the Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baillie_&_the_Boys "Baillie & the Boys"), [Paul Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Davis_(singer) "Paul Davis (singer)"), and [Paul Overstreet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Overstreet "Paul Overstreet").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-46) The album produced another number-one in "[Diggin' Up Bones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diggin'_Up_Bones "Diggin' Up Bones")" in late 1986, and a number two single in "[No Place Like Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Place_Like_Home_(Randy_Travis_song) "No Place Like Home (Randy Travis song)")" in early 1987. Overstreet wrote "On the Other Hand" with [Don Schlitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Schlitz "Don Schlitz"), "Diggin' Up Bones" with [Nat Stuckey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nat_Stuckey "Nat Stuckey"), and "No Place Like Home" by himself.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) The latter was also Travis's first single to be promoted through a [music video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video "Music video").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990116%E2%80%93117-47)

In late 1986, Travis was asked to host the [Country Music Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Music_Association "Country Music Association") (CMA) Awards telecast to replace original host [Ricky Skaggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Skaggs "Ricky Skaggs"), who had to back out after his son was hospitalized with a neck injury.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990109,_110-48) Travis won the Horizon Award (now called Best New Artist) at that ceremony, while also receiving a nomination for Male Vocalist of the Year. Additionally, "On the Other Hand" was nominated for Single of the Year and _Storms of Life_ for Album of the Year.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-cma-49) On November 15, 1986, Travis performed a concert with [George Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Jones "George Jones") and [Patty Loveless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patty_Loveless "Patty Loveless") in Charlotte, North Carolina, where Charlotte's then-mayor [Harvey Gantt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Gantt "Harvey Gantt") declared November 15 to be "Randy Travis Day". A similar acknowledgement was passed as a city ordinanace in Travis's hometown of Marshville soon afterward.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990112-50) Warner also issued a Christmas single in December 1986 titled "White Christmas Makes Me Blue", which sold over 79,000 copies.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990114-51) By year's end, Skaggs had inducted Travis into the Grand Ole Opry.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990115-52) "Diggin' Up Bones" also accounted for Travis's first [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award") nomination, in the category of [Best Male Country Vocal Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Male_Country_Vocal_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Male Country Vocal Performance"), in early 1987.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990121,_122-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-grammy-54)

_Storms of Life_ received critical favor. Mark A. Humphrey of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") wrote that Travis had "astonishing [Lefty Frizzell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lefty_Frizzell "Lefty Frizzell")-style pipes, excellent material, and sympathetic production".[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-storms_of_life-55) An uncredited review in _Billboard_ also described Travis's voice with favor, additionally stating that " He has the material—introspective lyrics and gorgeous melodies—and the understated, classic country production here to make the most of his gifts."[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-56) Writing for the _[Chicago Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago\_Tribune "Chicago Tribune")_, Jack Hurst also compared Travis's voice favorably to both Frizzell and [Merle Haggard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merle_Haggard "Merle Haggard"), while also praising the lyrics of the singles in particular.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-57)

### 1987–1988: _Always & Forever_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1987–1988: Always & Forever")]

In early 1987, Travis released the single "[Forever and Ever, Amen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forever_and_Ever,_Amen "Forever and Ever, Amen")". It held the number-one position on the _Billboard_ country charts for three weeks,[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990122-58) becoming the first song to hold that position for that long since [Johnny Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Lee_(singer) "Johnny Lee (singer)")'s "[Lookin' for Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lookin'_for_Love "Lookin' for Love")" in 1980.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoland1991490-59) The song served as the lead single to his second Warner album _[Always & Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Always\_&\_Forever\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Always & Forever (Randy Travis album)")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) As with "On the Other Hand", Schlitz and Overstreet co-wrote the song.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Corresponding with this song's success, Travis won Male Vocalist of the Year from the ACM awards, where _Storms of Life_ won Album of the Year and "On the Other Hand" won both Song and Single of the Year.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-acm-39) During the awards ceremony, Travis performed "Forever and Ever, Amen" live for the first time. Cusic described the song in 1990 as a "career record".[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990122-58) In addition to topping the country charts, "Forever and Ever, Amen" was a minor hit single in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), reaching number 55 on the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-60) In 2019, editors of _[The Tennessean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Tennessean "The Tennessean")_ listed it as one of the 100 greatest country songs of all time, while also referring to it as Travis's [signature song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signature_song "Signature song").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-61) "Forever and Ever, Amen" is also Travis's highest-certified single, having earned double-platinum RIAA certification in 2021.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-riaa-44)

[![Image 7: Randy Travis, wearing a gray suit while singing into a microphone](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Randy_Travis_MCI_Center_In_Washington.jpg/250px-Randy_Travis_MCI_Center_In_Washington.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Randy_Travis_MCI_Center_In_Washington.jpg)

Travis performing in 2003

_Always & Forever_ included Lehning as producer, with many of the same vocal and instrumental contributors as its predecessor such as Baillie & the Boys, Douglas, and Overstreet.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-62) Lehning worked with Travis, Hatcher, and Sharp to pick from several hundred songs before determining which ones would appear on the album.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990124-63) One track on the album was [Dennis Linde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Linde "Dennis Linde")'s composition "[What'll You Do About Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What'll_You_Do_About_Me "What'll You Do About Me")",[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990123-64) which was previously released by [Steve Earle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Earle "Steve Earle") in 1984;[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-earle-65) the song would later be released by [the Forester
