Sisters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Forester_Sisters "The Forester Sisters") in 1992,[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017130-66) and [Doug Supernaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doug_Supernaw "Doug Supernaw") in 1995.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017353-67) During the promotion of the album, Travis began to notice strain on his vocal cords, which was treated through consultations at [Vanderbilt University Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanderbilt_University_Medical_Center "Vanderbilt University Medical Center").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990125-68)_Always & Forever_ spent 43 weeks at the top of the _Billboard_[Top Country Albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_Country_Albums "Top Country Albums") charts, breaking the previous longevity record of 28 weeks set by [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama_(band) "Alabama (band)")'s _[Mountain Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain\_Music\_(Alabama\_album) "Mountain Music (Alabama album)")_ earlier in the decade.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoland1991490-59)

"[I Won't Need You Anymore (Always and Forever)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Won't_Need_You_Anymore_(Always_and_Forever) "I Won't Need You Anymore (Always and Forever)")", "[Too Gone Too Long](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Too_Gone_Too_Long "Too Gone Too Long")", and "[I Told You So](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Told_You_So_(Randy_Travis_song) "I Told You So (Randy Travis song)")" were all released as singles from _Always & Forever_, with all three reaching number one on the _Billboard_ country charts between 1987 and 1988.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Travis wrote "I Told You So" by himself in 1982 around the time he attempted to sign with Curb Records. Monk submitted the song to [Lee Greenwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Greenwood "Lee Greenwood") at that time, although he declined it. Both [Darrell Clanton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darrell_Clanton "Darrell Clanton") and Barbara Mandrell had recorded the song,[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic199042,_43,_63,_81-69) the former as the [B-side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-side "B-side") of his 1985 single "I Forgot That I Don't Live Here Anymore".[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn201783-70) In 1996, _Always & Forever_ received Travis's highest certification of quintuple platinum for sales of five million copies.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-riaa-44)

_Always & Forever_ and its singles accounted for several award wins and nominations for Travis. "Forever and Ever, Amen" won both Song and Single of the Year at the following year's ACM awards (honoring the year 1987), where Travis also won Top Male Vocalist. He was also nominated for Entertainer of the Year, while "Forever and Ever, Amen" received a Music Video of the Year nomination and _Always & Forever_ was nominated for Album of the Year.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-acm-39) At the 1987 CMA Awards, Travis won Male Vocalist of the Year and was nominated for Entertainer of the Year while "Forever and Ever, Amen" won Single of the Year and was nominated for Music Video of the Year and _Always & Forever_ won Album of the Year.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-cma-49) Additionally, _Always & Forever_ accounted for Travis's first Grammy Award win, for Best Male Country Vocal Performance at the [30th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/30th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "30th Annual Grammy Awards") in March 1988.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-grammy-54)[Stephen Thomas Erlewine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Thomas_Erlewine "Stephen Thomas Erlewine"), writing for AllMusic, thought the album "rivaled its predecessor in its quality" while also stating that it had "lean" production and "nuanced" vocals.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-71)

### 1988–1990: _Old 8×10_ and _No Holdin' Back_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1988–1990: Old 8×10 and No Holdin' Back")]

Travis continued to tour throughout the United States in 1988, including a spot on the [Marlboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlboro "Marlboro") Country Music Tour in [Madison Square Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Square_Garden "Madison Square Garden"), which also featured Alabama, [the Judds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Judds "The Judds"), and [George Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Strait "George Strait").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990150-72) That same year he released his third Warner album, _[Old 8×10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old\_8%C3%9710 "Old 8×10")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) The album was originally slated to be released on July 12, but was moved up to June 30 to make it eligible for CMA Awards.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTECusic1990152-73) The first three singles off the album all went to number one on the country charts between 1988 and early 1989. These were "[Honky Tonk Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honky_Tonk_Moon "Honky Tonk Moon")", "[Deeper Than the Holler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deeper_Than_the_Holler "Deeper Than the Holler")" (another Overstreet-Schlitz collaboration), and "[Is It Still Over?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is_It_Still_Over%3F "Is It Still Over?")"[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) The fourth and final single, "[Promises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promises_(Randy_Travis_song) "Promises (Randy Travis song)")" (which Travis wrote with John Lindley), was much less successful with a number 17 peak on Hot Country Songs.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Music journalists Tom Roland and [Colin Larkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Larkin "Colin Larkin") both attributed the song's failure to it featuring just vocals and acoustic guitar.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoland1991569,_570-74)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-virgin-11)_Old 8×10_ became his third consecutive album to reach the number one position on Top Country Albums.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-Country_Albums-75) It also won Travis a Grammy Award for Best Male Country Vocal Performance.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-grammy-54) "I Told You So" received a Single of the Year nomination from the Academy of Country Music, while Travis himself was nominated as both Entertainer of the Year and Top Male Vocalist in 1988 and 1989.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-acm-39) Also in 1988, the Country Music Association awarded him as Male Vocalist of the Year a second time, along with an Entertainer of the Year nomination, as well as Single and Song of the Year nominations for "I Told You So".[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-cma-49) The foundation also nominated _Old 8×10_ for Album of the Year alongside additional Male Vocalist and Entertainer of the Year nominations.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-cma-49) Reviewing the album for AllMusic, [Brian Mansfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Mansfield "Brian Mansfield") stated that it "lacks the monster hits of his debut but wears just as well."[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-76) In 1997, _Old 8×10_ received its highest certification of double-platinum.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-riaa-44)

[![Image 8: A black-and-white headshot of Brook Benton](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Brook_Benton_1959.jpg/250px-Brook_Benton_1959.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brook_Benton_1959.jpg)

Travis had a hit single in 1989 with a cover of "It's Just a Matter of Time", originally by Brook Benton (pictured in 1959).

Travis ended 1989 with two studio albums. First was a Christmas album titled _[An Old Time Christmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An\_Old\_Time\_Christmas "An Old Time Christmas")_, which included the previously released Christmas single "White Christmas Makes Me Blue". The other tracks included a mix of Christmas standards and original songs, one of which ("How Do I Wrap My Heart Up for Christmas") Travis co-wrote with Overstreet.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-77) A month later was the studio release _[No Holdin' Back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No\_Holdin'\_Back "No Holdin' Back")_. Prior to the album's release, Travis had recorded a cover of [Brook Benton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brook_Benton "Brook Benton")'s "[It's Just a Matter of Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Just_a_Matter_of_Time_(song) "It's Just a Matter of Time (song)")" with producer [Richard Perry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Perry "Richard Perry") for a covers album titled _Rock, Rhythm & Blues_. Because he liked the sound of the recording, he chose to include it on _No Holdin' Back_ as the album's first single. The rendition reached number one on the country charts in December 1989.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoland1991569%E2%80%93570-78) At the [32nd Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/32nd_Annual_Grammy_Awards "32nd Annual Grammy Awards"), this rendition was nominated for Best Male Country Vocal Performance.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-grammy-54) After the "It's Just a Matter of Time" cover came "[Hard Rock Bottom of Your Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_Rock_Bottom_of_Your_Heart "Hard Rock Bottom of Your Heart")". Written by [Hugh Prestwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Prestwood "Hugh Prestwood"), the song held the number one position on _Billboard_ Hot Country Songs for four weeks, accounting for Travis's longest stay at that position.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) The third and final single from _No Holdin' Back_ was "[He Walked on Water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/He_Walked_on_Water "He Walked on Water")", which peaked at number two.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) The song was the first successful cut for songwriter [Allen Shamblin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_Shamblin "Allen Shamblin").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-79) Also included on _No Holdin' Back_ were a cover of [Marty Robbins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Robbins "Marty Robbins")' "[Singing the Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singing_the_Blues "Singing the Blues")" and the track "[Somewhere in My Broken Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somewhere_in_My_Broken_Heart "Somewhere in My Broken Heart")", later a single for its co-writer [Billy Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Dean "Billy Dean").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017105-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-holdin-81) Thom Jurek's review for AllMusic praised Travis's vocal deliveries on "It's Just a Matter of Time" and "Hard Rock Bottom of Your Heart" while also calling Lehning's production "flawless".[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-holdin-81) In a review for _[Cash Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cash\_Box "Cash Box")_ magazine, Kimmy Wix described "He Walked on Water" as having "detailed lyrics to which we can all relate" and thought the song was well suited for Travis's voice.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-cashbox-82)

### 1990–1992: _Heroes & Friends_, _High Lonesome_, and greatest-hits albums

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1990–1992: Heroes & Friends, High Lonesome, and greatest-hits albums")]

Travis's first album to be released in the 1990s was _[Heroes & Friends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heroes\_&\_Friends "Heroes & Friends")_, a duets album. Among the duet artists featured were [Tammy Wynette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tammy_Wynette "Tammy Wynette"), [Merle Haggard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merle_Haggard "Merle Haggard"), [George Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Jones "George Jones"), [B. B. King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._B._King "B. B. King"), and [Clint Eastwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clint_Eastwood "Clint Eastwood").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-virgin-11) According to journalist Gary Graff, Travis had wanted to record a duet album for several years, and he and Hatcher spent over a year and a half arranging for the recording sessions.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-graff-83) The album accounted for two singles in "[A Few Ole Country Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Few_Ole_Country_Boys "A Few Ole Country Boys")" (a duet with Jones) and title track "[Heroes and Friends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heroes_and_Friends "Heroes and Friends")" (the only track on the album not to be a duet). Both songs peaked within the top 10 of the country charts between late 1990 and early 1991.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Travis performed "Heroes and Friends" at the 1991 CMA Awards telecast, joined by Jones, Wynette, [Vern Gosdin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vern_Gosdin "Vern Gosdin"), and [Roy Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Rogers "Roy Rogers").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019123-84) Unlike his previous albums, _Heroes & Friends_ was met with mixed reception from critics. _[Austin American-Statesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin\_American-Statesman "Austin American-Statesman")_ writer Lee Nichols thought that the album's songs were "not particularly notable, but nonetheless enjoyable".[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-85)[Knight Ridder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight_Ridder "Knight Ridder") writer Dan DeLuca (in a review re-published in _[The Anniston Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Anniston\_Star "The Anniston Star")_) praised the duets with Haggard and Jones, and considered the duet version of [Dolly Parton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolly_Parton "Dolly Parton")'s "[Do I Ever Cross Your Mind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Do_I_Ever_Cross_Your_Mind "Do I Ever Cross Your Mind")" to be the strongest track, although he also panned the contributions of King and Eastwood.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-86) In a review for _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment\_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_, [Alanna Nash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alanna_Nash "Alanna Nash") thought that "[t]he guests show up more to bolster Travis's profile than to actually perform full-out", although she praised [Loretta Lynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loretta_Lynn "Loretta Lynn")'s duet vocals on "Shopping for Dresses".[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-87) Despite the mixed reception, _Heroes & Friends_ certified platinum in 1991.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-riaa-44) Travis also noted that 1990 was the first year in which he did not receive any ACM or CMA awards, but that he was still receiving significant radio airplay and sales, and positive feedback from fans in concert.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-graff-83) Relatedly, Mansfield and [Colin Larkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Larkin "Colin Larkin") both observed that in the early 1990s, Travis's success began to diminish as newer artists such as [Clint Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clint_Black "Clint Black") and [Garth Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garth_Brooks "Garth Brooks") grew in popularity.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-virgin-11)

[![Image 9: A head shot of Alan Jackson, wearing a cowboy hat and sunglasses](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/AlanJacksonApr10.jpg/250px-AlanJacksonApr10.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AlanJacksonApr10.jpg)

Alan Jackson co-wrote several songs on Travis's 1991 album _High Lonesome_.

Travis's next studio album was 1991's _[High Lonesome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High\_Lonesome\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "High Lonesome (Randy Travis album)")_, led off by the single "[Point of Light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_of_Light "Point of Light")".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1)[George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush"), then [President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States"), commissioned Schlitz and [Thom Schuyler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thom_Schuyler "Thom Schuyler") to write the song as a tie-in to his "[thousand points of light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thousand_points_of_light "Thousand points of light")" campaign for [volunteerism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volunteerism "Volunteerism").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019115-88) Because of its inspiration, Travis noted that journalists often asked him about political matters, and he refused to answer them as he did not think the song itself was political.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-89) He also performed the song for a number of events intended to honor American soldiers returning from [Operation Desert Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Desert_Storm "Operation Desert Storm").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019115,_116-90) Next from _High Lonesome_ was Travis's twelfth number-one, "[Forever Together](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forever_Together "Forever Together")",[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) one of several songs he wrote with [Alan Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Jackson "Alan Jackson") while the two were on tour together in 1991.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-bernard-91) These collaborations also produced the album's next two singles "[Better Class of Losers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Better_Class_of_Losers "Better Class of Losers")" and "[I'd Surrender All](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'd_Surrender_All "I'd Surrender All")" between late 1991 and early 1992, as well as Jackson's number one single "[She's Got the Rhythm (And I Got the Blues)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/She's_Got_the_Rhythm_(And_I_Got_the_Blues) "She's Got the Rhythm (And I Got the Blues)")" later in 1992.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019124-92) Jackson also co-wrote the track "Allergic to the Blues", while Travis wrote "I'm Gonna Have a Little Talk" (featuring backing vocals from gospel group [Take 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take_6 "Take 6")[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-jurek_high-93)) and "Oh, What a Time to Be Me". Travis noted that the project contained more songs written by him than his previous ones did.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-bernard-91) Jurek praised the Jackson co-writes in particular, highlighting their lyrics and vocal deliveries in his review for AllMusic.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-jurek_high-93) Nash also praised the lyrics on the songs co-written by Jackson, while also stating that Travis "never sounded so relaxed or so confident".[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-nash_lonesome-94)

Later the same year, Warner released a pair of [greatest hits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest_hits "Greatest hits") albums: _[Greatest Hits, Volume One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest\_Hits,\_Volume\_One\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Greatest Hits, Volume One (Randy Travis album)")_ and _[Greatest Hits, Volume Two](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest\_Hits,\_Volume\_Two\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Greatest Hits, Volume Two (Randy Travis album)")_. In addition to featuring most of his hit singles to this point, the projects also included four new tracks and the album cut "Reasons I Cheat" from _Storms of Life_.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-beyer-95) Among the new tracks, "[If I Didn't Have You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_I_Didn't_Have_You_(Randy_Travis_song) "If I Didn't Have You (Randy Travis song)")" and "[Look Heart, No Hands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Look_Heart,_No_Hands "Look Heart, No Hands")" both went to number one upon release as singles that year. [Skip Ewing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skip_Ewing "Skip Ewing") and [Max D. Barnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_D._Barnes "Max D. Barnes") wrote the former, while [Trey Bruce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trey_Bruce "Trey Bruce") and [Russell Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Smith_(singer) "Russell Smith (singer)") wrote the latter.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Despite these songs' successes on radio, their follow-up "[An Old Pair of Shoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Old_Pair_of_Shoes "An Old Pair of Shoes")" reached number 21 upon release in early 1993.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Both greatest-hits albums certified platinum in 1995.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-riaa-44)

### 1992–1995: _Wind in the Wire_ and _This Is Me_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 1992–1995: Wind in the Wire and This Is Me")]

Travis took a hiatus from touring in 1992 and 1993, citing exhaustion as the reason for doing so.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019126-96) He and Hatcher chose to spend time at a property in [Maui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui "Maui") they had acquired. According to Travis, the touring hiatus caused some fans and news reporters to believe he had retired,[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-new_album-97) so his publicists issued press releases indicating he was "merely taking a break".[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019127-98) During the hiatus, he released an album of [Western music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_music_(North_America) "Western music (North America)") titled _[Wind in the Wire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind\_in\_the\_Wire "Wind in the Wire")_, a tie-in to a television movie [of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_in_the_Wire_(film) "Wind in the Wire (film)") in which he starred.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) The album was produced by session guitarist Steve Gibson, making it his first since the Randy Ray album not to be produced by Kyle Lehning.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019130-99) It was commercially unsuccessful, with none of its singles reaching top 40 on the _Billboard_ charts.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) However, lead single "[Cowboy Boogie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowboy_Boogie "Cowboy Boogie")" reached number 10 on the Canadian country music charts then published by _[RPM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RPM\_(magazine) "RPM (magazine)")_.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-100) Travis and one of his managers later attributed the album's commercial failure to its [Western swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_swing "Western swing") sound proving unpopular with radio.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-new_album-97)

In late 1993, Travis began working on a follow-up album with Lehning when he was contacted by a representative for the then-under construction [MGM Grand Las Vegas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MGM_Grand_Las_Vegas "MGM Grand Las Vegas") in [Las Vegas, Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Vegas,_Nevada "Las Vegas, Nevada"). The representative wanted Travis to be the first country artist to perform at the new venue once it opened, which inspired Travis to begin touring again. He and Hatcher joined with Jeff Davis, another former manager of Travis's who was then working with [Brother Phelps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brother_Phelps "Brother Phelps"), to assemble a backing band for the Las Vegas shows, which included Lehning as keyboardist.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019131,_132-101) The Las Vegas shows, held in early 1994, were his first concerts in over 14 months.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-new_album-97) Due to the success of these shows, Travis resumed his touring schedule soon afterward. He re-established his existing touring band and performed at a showcase of Warner Bros. artists held in Nashville during the Country Radio Seminar, an annual promotional concert series held by [Country Radio Broadcasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Radio_Broadcasters "Country Radio Broadcasters").[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019131,_132-101)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-new_album-97) At the same time, Travis continued writing and compiling songs for his next studio album. "[Before You Kill Us All](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Before_You_Kill_Us_All "Before You Kill Us All")" was released on February 28, 1994,[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-new_album-97) as the lead single to his next Warner album _[This Is Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This\_Is\_Me\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "This Is Me (Randy Travis album)")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) The song peaked at number two on the _Billboard_ country charts.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Travis and Lehning chose the song because the two wanted "story songs and some with a wink of humor".[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019133-102) Similarly, he told _Billboard_ in 1994 that the song was an example of a more modern and "rowdy" sound he wanted to achieve relative to his prior albums.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-new_album-97) It was followed later in the year by "[Whisper My Name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whisper_My_Name "Whisper My Name")", his fifteenth number-one on _Billboard_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) The album's [title track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This_Is_Me_(Randy_Travis_song) "This Is Me (Randy Travis song)") and "[The Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Box_(Randy_Travis_song) "The Box (Randy Travis song)")" were both top-ten hits between late 1994 and early 1995 as well.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Travis wrote "The Box" with Buck Moore and later said he became emotional writing and performing the song, as its theme of a father struggling to express love to his children reminded him of his own "fractured" relationship with his father.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019133-102)

Bob Saporiti, then an executive at Warner Bros. Nashville, noted that the failure of _Wind in the Wire_ and length of time since _High Lonesome_ had created "angst" among label executives, but added that they considered _This Is Me_ "back to the basics".[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-new_album-97) To promote the album, Travis hosted an episode of the TNN talk show _Music City Tonight_; the network also re-aired the Country Radio Seminar concert.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-new_album-97) Jurek praised the lyrical contributions of Trey Bruce, [Larry Gatlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Gatlin "Larry Gatlin"), and [Kieran Kane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kieran_Kane "Kieran Kane"), and considered "Whisper My Name" to be "among the greatest songs Travis has ever recorded".[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-103) Nash thought that the lyrics of the singles were among Travis's strongest, also stating that the album had "zippier instrumental touches" than his 1980s albums.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-104) Additionally, Larkin stated that the album was "as strong as ever".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-virgin-11) By mid-1994, _This Is Me_ was certified gold by the RIAA.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-riaa-44) Despite spending most of 1995 without a charted single,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Travis continued to tour throughout the year alongside [Sammy Kershaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Kershaw "Sammy Kershaw") and George Jones.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019135-105)

### 1996–1997: _Full Circle_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 1996–1997: Full Circle")]

[![Image 10: Mark Knopfler playing an electric guitar](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Mar-Knopfler-Pensa-Blue.jpg/250px-Mar-Knopfler-Pensa-Blue.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mar-Knopfler-Pensa-Blue.jpg)

Mark Knopfler wrote Travis's 1996 single "Are We in Trouble Now".

Travis's final album for Warner was _[Full Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full\_Circle\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Full Circle (Randy Travis album)")_ in 1996.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) Travis told _Billboard_ prior to its release that he and Lehning spent over a year selecting songs for the album because they wanted to be sure they were fully satisfied with its content.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-full_circle-106) Its lead single was "[Are We in Trouble Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Are_We_in_Trouble_Now "Are We in Trouble Now")", a song written by [Mark Knopfler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Knopfler "Mark Knopfler"). Both this song and follow-up "[Would I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Would_I "Would I")" failed to reach the top 20 on the country charts, while neither "Price to Pay" nor a cover of [Roger Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Miller "Roger Miller")'s "[King of the Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_the_Road_(song) "King of the Road (song)")" (which also appeared on the soundtrack of the 1997 movie _[Traveller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traveller\_(1997\_film) "Traveller (1997 film)")_[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-107)) made top 40.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1)_[Richmond Times-Dispatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond\_Times-Dispatch "Richmond Times-Dispatch")_ writer Gordon Ely noted the failure of the album's lead single and questioned whether the album and Travis in general could still be successful in the long term, due to an influx of younger artists in the intervening years.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-gordon-108) Ely considered the album "strong as ever", with a focus on Lehning's production and Travis's voice, as well as the lyrics of "Price to Pay".[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-gordon-108)[Country Standard Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Standard_Time "Country Standard Time") writer Don Yates found the influence of [honky-tonk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honky-tonk "Honky-tonk") in certain songs and praised the lyrics and vocal delivery of "Are We in Trouble Now", but criticized "Would I" as "gimmicky" and closing track "Ants on a Log" as "trite".[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-109) AllMusic writer Thom Owens said of _Full Circle_, "his mid-'90s albums suffered from a tendency to sound a bit too similar to each other. _Full Circle_ solves that problem by simultaneously reaching back into his hardcore honky-tonk roots and moving toward more contemporary material".[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-110)

In mid-1997, Travis announced that he had departed from Warner Bros. due to disagreements over the promotion of _Full Circle_, as well as concerns that the country music industry was beginning to move toward back [country pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_pop "Country pop") influences.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-travels-111) Additionally, Hatcher thought that Warner executives were not allowing her, Travis, and Lehning to have as much liberty on selecting singles as they had on previous albums.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019142-112) At the time of his departure from Warner, Travis was offered contracts by the Nashville divisions of both [Asylum Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asylum_Records "Asylum Records") and the then-new [DreamWorks Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DreamWorks_Records "DreamWorks Records").[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-travels-111) Lehning had just become president of Asylum Records's Nashville division at the time, but Travis chose not to follow him to that label as he did not think Lehning's position was long-term.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019143-113)

### 1997–1999: DreamWorks Records

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 1997–1999: DreamWorks Records")]

By August 1997, Travis had become the first artist signed to DreamWorks Records's Nashville division.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-114) The new label's president was musician and producer James Stroud, who had played on some of Travis' singles, including "Forever and Ever, Amen".[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019135,_136,_142-115) As Lehning's duties at Asylum left him temporarily unavailable, Stroud and [Byron Gallimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byron_Gallimore "Byron Gallimore") produced Travis for DreamWorks.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019143-113) "[Out of My Bones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_My_Bones "Out of My Bones")" was the first single release for DreamWorks Nashville, in 1997.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-116) Co-written by [Gary Burr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Burr "Gary Burr") and [Sharon Vaughn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharon_Vaughn "Sharon Vaughn"), it peaked at number two on the country charts early in 1998.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) It appeared on his first DreamWorks album _[You and You Alone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You\_and\_You\_Alone\_(album) "You and You Alone (album)")_, issued in April.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) The project also accounted for the top-ten hits "[The Hole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hole_(song) "The Hole (song)")" and "[Spirit of a Boy, Wisdom of a Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_of_a_Boy,_Wisdom_of_a_Man "Spirit of a Boy, Wisdom of a Man")" and the top-20 "[Stranger in My Mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stranger_in_My_Mirror "Stranger in My Mirror")". Both "The Hole" and "Stranger in My Mirror" were co-written by Skip Ewing.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) "Spirit of a Boy, Wisdom of a Man" was previously recorded by [Mark Collie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Collie "Mark Collie") on his 1995 album _[Tennessee Plates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee\_Plates "Tennessee Plates")_.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-117) Jeffrey B. Remz of Country Standard Time criticized the heavy drums on "I Did My Part", but otherwise praised the use of acoustic instruments and the strength of Travis's voice.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-remz_alone-118)_[Lincoln Journal Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln\_Journal\_Star "Lincoln Journal Star")_ writer L. Kent Wolgamott noted the presence of [fiddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiddle "Fiddle") and [steel guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel_guitar "Steel guitar") in the production while also calling Travis's voice "expressive".[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-lincoln-119)

In 1999, Travis was one of several artists on the collaborative song "Same Old Train", featured on the multi-artist album _[Tribute to Tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribute\_to\_Tradition "Tribute to Tradition")_. Other acts appearing on the song included [Clint Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clint_Black "Clint Black"), [Dwight Yoakam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_Yoakam "Dwight Yoakam"), and [Pam Tillis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pam_Tillis "Pam Tillis"), along with [Marty Stuart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Stuart "Marty Stuart"), who wrote and produced it.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-120) The track won a [Grammy Award for Best Country Collaboration with Vocals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Country_Collaboration_with_Vocals "Grammy Award for Best Country Collaboration with Vocals").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-grammy-54) Travis's second and final DreamWorks album _[A Man Ain't Made of Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Man\_Ain't\_Made\_of\_Stone "A Man Ain't Made of Stone")_ released in 1999.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14)[The title track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Man_Ain't_Made_of_Stone_(song) "A Man Ain't Made of Stone (song)") (co-written by Burr) was a top-20 country hit by year's end, but the other singles, "Where Can I Surrender", "A Little Left of Center", and "I'll Be Right Here Loving You", all missed the top 40.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Gallimore and Stroud recorded the album largely in [Santa Fe, New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Fe,_New_Mexico "Santa Fe, New Mexico"), where Travis and Hatcher had a house at the time.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-121) Following the failure of the later singles, Travis exited DreamWorks in 2000.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-122) Shortly after his departure, Travis told Country Standard Time that he chose to leave DreamWorks because he felt the label had not properly distributed the album. He added that Stroud's production style put too much emphasis on instrumentation instead of his singing voice.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-inspiration-123)

### 2000–2003: Switch to gospel and "Three Wooden Crosses"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 2000–2003: Switch to gospel and \"Three Wooden Crosses\"")]

[![Image 11: Kenny Chesney, singing with one arm extended and the other holding a microphone](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Kenny_Chesney_20070830.jpg/250px-Kenny_Chesney_20070830.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kenny_Chesney_20070830.jpg)

Kenny Chesney (pictured in 2007) collaborated with Travis on the 2000 single "Baptism".

While he was still on Warner, Travis had begun working with Lehning on a [gospel music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music") album.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-inspirational_allmusic-124)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-125) Other than a cover of "[Amazing Grace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazing_Grace "Amazing Grace")", the two intentionally sought to include original content. Travis finished the tracks at a time when he was not on a record label. Through a connection Lehning had with [Word Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_Records "Word Records") executive Barry Landis, Travis was signed to that label in late 2000 and released the gospel album, by then titled _[Inspirational Journey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inspirational\_Journey "Inspirational Journey")_.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019149,_150-126)[Waylon Jennings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waylon_Jennings "Waylon Jennings") and [Jessi Colter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessi_Colter "Jessi Colter") provided guest vocals on "The Carpenter".[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-inspirational_allmusic-124)[Kenny Chesney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Chesney "Kenny Chesney") sang duet vocals on "[Baptism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptism_(Kenny_Chesney_and_Randy_Travis_song) "Baptism (Kenny Chesney and Randy Travis song)")" (also titled "Down with the Old Man (Up with the New)"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-127) which served as the first single. The two had previously recorded the song for Chesney's 1999 album _[Everywhere We Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everywhere\_We\_Go "Everywhere We Go")_.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-inspiration-123)_Inspirational Journey_ won two [Dove Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dove_Awards "Dove Awards") in 2001: Bluegrass Album of the Year for the album itself, and Country Recorded Song of the Year for "Baptism".[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-dove-128) AllMusic reviewer Todd Everett found influences of bluegrass, [Don Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Williams "Don Williams"), and Lefty Frizzell, and found it consistent with Travis's 1980s and 1990s albums in tone.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-inspirational_allmusic-124) Alanna Nash of _Entertainment Weekly_ was less favorable, as she thought that the album had strong opening tracks but added that "midway, it deteriorates into Nashville formula, with simplistic homilies [and] overblown production".[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-129)

Following the [September 11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks") in 2001, Travis co-wrote and released a promotional patriotic single titled "America Will Always Stand".[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-130) Proceeds from sales of the single were donated to the [American Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Red_Cross "American Red Cross").[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-131) He continued with Word as a gospel artist and put out his next album for the label, _[Rise and Shine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rise\_and\_Shine\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Rise and Shine (Randy Travis album)")_, in 2002. The lead single was "[Three Wooden Crosses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Wooden_Crosses "Three Wooden Crosses")". According to Travis, songwriters [Kim Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Williams_(songwriter) "Kim Williams (songwriter)") and [Doug Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doug_Johnson_(record_producer) "Doug Johnson (record producer)") had pitched the song to [Michael Peterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Peterson_(singer) "Michael Peterson (singer)"), who at the time was recording with Lehning. Peterson suggested Lehning take the song to Travis, for whom he thought it was better suited.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019152,_153-132) By early 2003, "Three Wooden Crosses" became Travis's sixteenth and final number-one on _Billboard_ Hot Country Songs. It also accounted for his highest solo peak on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") at number 31. The project charted one other single in "Pray for the Fish", which fell below top 40 on the country charts.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Robert L. Doerschuk of AllMusic called the album "a strong performance, presented with flawless studio clarity and persuasive, understated feeling."[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-robert-133) Remz noted the consistency of Lehning's production and Travis's voice, as well as the presence of original songs co-written by Travis.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-134) In October 2003, _Rise and Shine_ was certified gold.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-riaa-44) At the 2004 Grammy Awards, _Rise and Shine_ won a [Grammy Award for Best Southern, Country or Bluegrass Gospel Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Southern,_Country_or_Bluegrass_Gospel_Album "Grammy Award for Best Southern, Country or Bluegrass Gospel Album"), while "Three Wooden Crosses" was nominated for Best Male Country Vocal Performance.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-grammy-54) That same year, "Pray for the Fish" won a Dove Award for Country Recorded Song of the Year.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-dove-128)

### 2003–2007: Continued gospel albums

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 2003–2007: Continued gospel albums")]

His next gospel album was 2003's _[Worship & Faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worship\_&\_Faith "Worship & Faith")_. Unlike the previous projects, it included 20 acoustic covers of existing praise songs and hymns.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-135) Among the tracks included were "[In the Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_the_Garden_(1912_song) "In the Garden (1912 song)")", "[How Great Thou Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How_Great_Thou_Art "How Great Thou Art")", "[Peace in the Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_in_the_Valley "Peace in the Valley")", and "[I'll Fly Away](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'll_Fly_Away "I'll Fly Away")". Jurek called the album "direct, unfiltered, hard-line gospel at its best, by a master" in a review for AllMusic.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-136)_Worship & Faith_ also became a gold album,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-riaa-44) and accounted for his second consecutive Grammy Award for Best Southern, Country or Bluegrass Gospel Album.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-grammy-54) A year later he released _[Passing Through](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passing\_Through\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Passing Through (Randy Travis album)")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) This album accounted for his last solo chart singles until 2024, "Four Walls" and "Angels".[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019152,_153-132) The latter was Travis's 50th entry on the chart.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366-1) Co-writers on the album included [Jamie O'Hara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamie_O'Hara_(singer) "Jamie O'Hara (singer)"), Dennis Linde, Sharon Vaughn, and Travis.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-passing-137) "Four Walls" was previously cut by [Keith Harling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Harling "Keith Harling"),[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-138) while the album track "That Was Us" was previously recorded by both [Tracy Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracy_Lawrence "Tracy Lawrence") and [Chad Brock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chad_Brock "Chad Brock"), whose version was a single in 2003.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-139)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-passing-137)[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn201753-140) Erlewine wrote of _Passing Through_, "It's inspirational music in the purest sense—it doesn't preach, it instructs and inspires through its carefully observed tales."[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-passing-137) Travis received a star on the [Hollywood Walk of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_Walk_of_Fame "Hollywood Walk of Fame") in September 2004.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-141)

In 2005, Travis released another gospel album, _[Glory Train: Songs of Faith, Worship, and Praise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glory\_Train:\_Songs\_of\_Faith,\_Worship,\_and\_Praise "Glory Train: Songs of Faith, Worship, and Praise")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) It, too, won a Grammy Award for Best Southern, Country or Bluegrass Gospel Album.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-grammy-54) Some tracks on the project included backing vocals from [the Blind Boys of Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blind_Boys_of_Alabama "The Blind Boys of Alabama"). Unlike the previous albums, it contained a mix of Black spirituals and [contemporary Christian music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Christian_music "Contemporary Christian music") such as [Darlene Zschech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darlene_Zschech "Darlene Zschech")'s "[Shout to the Lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shout_to_the_Lord "Shout to the Lord")". Erlewine thought the inclusion of such material made it "Travis's best gospel album to date".[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-142) Writing for _[The Atlanta Journal-Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Atlanta\_Journal-Constitution "The Atlanta Journal-Constitution")_, Nick Marino praised Travis's "[bluesy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues")" vocals and the variety of songs.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-143) Altogether, Travis's first four gospel albums each won the Dove Award for Country Album of the Year, accounting for a streak of four consecutive wins in that category from 2003 to 2006.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-dove-128) Also in 2006, Travis began recording footage for a Christmas DVD titled _Christmas on the Pecos_. This footage consisted of him singing Christmas songs and reading [Helen Steiner Rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Steiner_Rice "Helen Steiner Rice")'s poem "The Christmas Guest" inside the Big Room, a cavern at [Carlsbad Caverns National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlsbad_Caverns_National_Park "Carlsbad Caverns National Park").[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019160,_161-144)[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-145) Some of the performances also included vocal accompaniment from the choir of the Carlsbad First Baptist Church. The DVD was released in late 2006.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019160,_161-144) Another Christmas project, the album _[Songs of the Season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songs\_of\_the\_Season "Songs of the Season")_, followed in 2007.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-146)

### 2008–2011: Return to Warner and Carrie Underwood version of "I Told You So"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Randy_Travis&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 2008–2011: Return to Warner and Carrie Underwood version of \"I Told You So\"")]

In 2008, he released his next studio album _[Around the Bend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Around\_the\_Bend\_(album) "Around the Bend (album)")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-allmusic-14) The project was his first country music release since _A Man Ain't Made of Stone_.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019165-147)[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-jeff-148) The album also placed him back on Warner, which had been a distributor of his Word Records releases.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-149) Travis promoted the album in an interview with [WSM-FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSM-FM "WSM-FM") radio host [Bill Cody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Cody_(radio_host) "Bill Cody (radio host)").[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019165-147) He also released its lead single "Faith in You" as a free download from his website.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-150) "Dig Two Graves" was the project's second single.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-jeff-148) In addition to these songs, the album included a cover of [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan")'s "[Don't Think Twice, It's All Right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Think_Twice,_It's_All_Right "Don't Think Twice, It's All Right")".[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTETravisAbraham2019165-147) Jeff DeDekker of _[The Leader-Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Leader-Post "The Leader-Post")_ noted that while it was not marketed as a Christian album, individual songs still held themes of "redemption and the afterlife".[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-jeff-148) He praised the lyrics of "Dig Two Graves" and Travis's singing voice in particular.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-jeff-148) Erlewine criticized the use of a [string section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_section "String section") on "Faith in You", but otherwise reviewed the album's song selection and Travis's voice with favor.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-bend-151) Despite not being explicitly marketed as a Christian album, it won Travis his eighth and final Dove Award, in the category of Country Album of the Year.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-dove-128)

[![Image 12: A bust shot of Carrie Underwood in a purple dress](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/191125_Carrie_Underwood_at_the_2019_American_Music_Awards.png/250px-191125_Carrie_Underwood_at_the_2019_American_Music_Awards.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:191125_Carrie_Underwood_at_the_2019_American_Music_Awards.png)

Carrie Underwood had a hit in 2009 with a rendition of Travis's "I Told You So".

[Carrie Underwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrie_Underwood "Carrie Underwood") recorded a cover of "I Told You So" on her late-2007 album _[Carnival Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnival\_Ride "Carnival Ride")_.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-152) Her version was released in January 2009 as the album's fifth single. Two months after her rendition was released to radio, disc jockey Jesse Tack at [WUBE-FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WUBE-FM "WUBE-FM") in [Cincinnati, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati,_Ohio "Cincinnati, Ohio") combined Underwood's recording with the vocal track from Travis's original and distributed the results to 75 other radio stations. Due to the popularity of the combined recording with radio listeners, Underwood and Travis performed the song together on _[American Idol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Idol "American Idol")_ soon after.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-153) The two also recorded an official duet version, which was sent to radio as well.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-154) With both Travis and Underwood receiving chart credit, the duet version of "I Told You So" peaked at number two on the country charts in 2009, and accounted for Travis's highest overall _Billboard_ Hot 100 peak of number nine.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitburn2017365,_366,_374,_375-155) The duet won both artists the 2010 Grammy Award for Best Country Collaboration with Vocals.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Travis_discography#cite_note-grammy-54)

Travis continued to record for Warner at the time. Randy Travis is an American [country music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") singer. His albums [discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discography "Discography") comprises 23 [studio albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album "Album"), including two holiday albums, 17 [compilation albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compilation_album "Compilation album"), and two [live albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_album "Live album"). His first six studio releases have all been certified platinum or higher by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America"), with the highest-certified being 1987's _[Always & Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Always\_&\_Forever\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Always & Forever (Randy Travis album)")_, at 5× Platinum certification for shipments of five million copies. Four more studio albums, including his first holiday album, have been certified gold, and his first two Greatest Hits packages are each certified platinum.

Randy Travis is an American [country music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") singer. His albums [discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discography "Discography") comprises 23 [studio albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album "Album"), including two holiday albums, 17 [compilation albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compilation_album "Compilation album"), and two [live albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_album "Live album"). His first six studio releases have all been certified platinum or higher by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America"), with the highest-certified being 1987's _[Always & Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Always\_&\_Forever\_(Randy\_Travis\_album) "Always & Forever (Randy Travis album)")_, at 5× Platinum certification for shipments of five million copies. Four more studio albums, including his first holiday album, have been certified gold, and his first two Greatest Hits packages are each certified platinum.

_**Portland**_ is a studio album by [Kevin Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician) "Kevin Burke (musician)") and [Mícheál Ó Domhnaill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%ADche%C3%A1l_%C3%93_Domhnaill "Mícheál Ó Domhnaill"), released in 1982 by [Green Linnet Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Linnet_Records "Green Linnet Records") (SIF 1041).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-discogs-1) This is the second and final album by this duo who first played together with the popular Irish traditional group [The Bothy Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bothy_Band "The Bothy Band").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-harris-2)

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Portland_(album)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

Mícheál Ó Domhnaill co-founded the popular Irish traditional group [The Bothy Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bothy_Band "The Bothy Band") in 1974, along with [Paddy Glackin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddy_Glackin "Paddy Glackin") (fiddle), [Matt Molloy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Molloy "Matt Molloy") (flute and tin whistle), [Paddy Keenan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddy_Keenan "Paddy Keenan") ([uilleann pipes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uilleann_pipes "Uilleann pipes") and tin whistle), [Dónal Lunny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%B3nal_Lunny "Dónal Lunny") (bouzouki, guitar, and production), and his sister [Tríona Ní Dhomhnaill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tr%C3%ADona_N%C3%AD_Dhomhnaill "Tríona Ní Dhomhnaill") ([harpsichord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpsichord "Harpsichord"), [clavinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clavinet "Clavinet") and vocals). Ó Domhnaill met [Kevin Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician) "Kevin Burke (musician)") when Burke replaced Glackin in the Bothy Band in May 1976. In the five years the Bothy Band were together, they emerged as one of the most exciting groups in the history of [Irish traditional music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music_of_Ireland "Folk music of Ireland"). Much of their repertoire was rooted in the traditional music of Ireland, and their enthusiasm and musical virtuosity set a standard for future Irish traditional performers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-harris-2) They recorded three studio albums during their brief career: _The Bothy Band_ (1975), _Old Hag You Have Killed Me_ (1976), and _Out of the Wind – Into the Sun_ (1977). A live album _After Hours_ was released in 1979, the year the group disbanded.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-harris-2)

When the Bothy Band disbanded in 1979, Burke and Ó Domhnaill toured the United Kingdom and Europe together, and recorded a highly acclaimed album, _[Promenade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promenade\_(1979\_album) "Promenade (1979 album)")_ (1979).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-harris-2) In 1980, Burke and Ó Domhnaill moved to the United States and toured extensively throughout the country.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-harris-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-tg4-doc-1-3) After settling in Portland, Oregon, the two recorded this second and final album together in 1982.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-tg4-doc-1-3) They continued to perform together the following year, but eventually parted ways to pursue other musical opportunities. Ó Domhnaill went on to form the popular group [Nightnoise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nightnoise "Nightnoise") with his sister [Tríona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tr%C3%ADona_N%C3%AD_Dhomhnaill "Tríona Ní Dhomhnaill"), [Billy Oskay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Oskay "Billy Oskay"), and Brian Dunning; he lived in Portland until 1997, when he returned to Ireland. He passed away on July 7, 2006. In addition to his acclaimed solo albums, Burke went on to form the influential Celtic groups Patrick Street and the [Celtic Fiddle Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtic_Fiddle_Festival "Celtic Fiddle Festival"), as well as successful collaborations with [Jackie Daly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Daly "Jackie Daly") and Cal Scott.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-wmc-4) Burke still lives in Portland and continues to tour throughout the world.

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Portland_(album)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Production")]

_Portland_ was recorded in Portland, Oregon in 1982.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-oregan-5) The instrumentation is restricted to Burke on fiddle, and Ó Domhnaill on vocals, guitar, and harmonium.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6)

## Composition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Portland_(album)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Composition")]

_Portland_ consists of nine tracks, five of which are medleys. The first track consists of three [reels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reel_(dance) "Reel (dance)"): "Maudabawn Chapel", was written by Ed Reavy, was learned from Martin Byrnes; "The Wild Irishman" was learned from Michael Coleman, and "The Moher Reel" was learned from Lucy Farr.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6) "Éirigh A Shiúir" is a traditional song that Ó Domhnaill learned from his aunt Neilí, a renowned singer who had a vast repertoire of Irish and English songs.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-oregan-5) The song is bout a shepherd who invites his true love to elope with him.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6) "Breton Gavottes" consists of three dances, the first and third of which are traditional, the second was written by Padrig Sicard.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6) The fourth track consists of three traditional tunes: "The Rolling Waves", "The Market Town", and "Scatter the Mud"—the latter two were learned through _O'Neill's Music of Ireland_ (1903), compiled by [Francis O'Neill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_O'Neill "Francis O'Neill"), an Irish-born American police officer and collector of Irish traditional music.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6) "Aird Uí Chumhaing" is another traditional Irish song that Ó Domhnaill learned from father, Aodh Ó Domhnaill, a teacher, a singer, and a collector of traditional music for the Irish Folklore Commission. The title refers to a townland on the northeast coast of Ireland. The song is about an exile from Aird Uí Chumhaing who looks across at his native coastline from the Mull of Kintre in Scotland and dreams of finding a boat that will carry him back to his childhood home, where he longs to live out the rest of his days.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6)

The sixth track is another medley of reels: "Paddy's Return" learned from the [Tulla Céilí Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tulla_C%C3%A9il%C3%AD_Band "The Tulla Céilí Band"), "Willy Coleman's", written by Willy Coleman who came from [County Sligo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Sligo "County Sligo"), and "Up in the Air", written by Burke and Ó Domhnaill.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6) The seventh track also consists of three reels: "Lucy's Fling" was written by Lucy Farr, "S'iomadh Rud A Chunnaic Mi", a piece of mouth music in Scottish Gaelic, was learned from Finlay MacNeill, and "Some Say the Devil is Dead", a traditional tune.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6) "Is Fada Liom Uaim Í" is another traditional song that Ó Domhnaill learned from his aunt Neilí. The song is about a man who complains that the woman he desires is beyond his reach.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6) The album's ninth and final track is a medley of four tunes: "Tom Morrison's" was written by Tom Morrison, "The Beare Island Reel" was learned from Dale Russ, "George White's Favourite" was learned from Paddy Killoran, and "Dipping the Sheep" was learned from _O'Neill's Music of Ireland_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6)

Ó Domhnaill and Burke have been called "one of the finest duets ever recorded in Irish traditional music".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-hitchner-8) In contrast to the "propulsive power and bracing brinkmanship" produced by the Bothy Band, the duo set off on a different musical path that one reviewer from the _Irish Echo_ called "soulful finesse".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-hitchner-8)

> Their sound was unrushed, detailed, spellbindingly beautiful, yet still pulsing with vitality. For tunes, it was the ultimate rhythmic glide, smooth rather than slick, without a hint of coasting. For songs, it was respect and reflection conveyed with absolute conviction.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-hitchner-8)

Ó Domhnaill's guitar playing and Burke's Sligo-style Irish fiddling achieved a "relaxed vitality" through "compelling melodies, pulsing Sligo rhythms, intricate variations, and vocal perfection".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-linnet-9) Reviewers singled out the "tender, baring passion" of Ó Domhnaill's voice in his renditions of "Eirigh a Shiuir" and "Aird Ui Chumhaing".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-hitchner-8)

> He treated traditional songs in Irish as the enduring testament of history handed down by those who experienced it rather than merely documented it. His acoustic guitar playing was, like himself, unobtrusive yet intense, focused on gimmick-free impact and ever-mindful that it must support, not supplant, Burke's melodic fiddling.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-hitchner-8)

In his review for AllMusic, Steve Winick called the album "another fine display" by Burke and Ó Domhnaill, giving the album four and a half out of five stars.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-allmusic-review-7)
