_**Portland**_ is a studio album by [Kevin Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician) "Kevin Burke (musician)") and [Mícheál Ó Domhnaill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%ADche%C3%A1l_%C3%93_Domhnaill "Mícheál Ó Domhnaill"), released in 1982 by [Green Linnet Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Linnet_Records "Green Linnet Records") (SIF 1041).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-discogs-1) This is the second and final album by this duo who first played together with the popular Irish traditional group [The Bothy Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bothy_Band "The Bothy Band").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-harris-2)

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Portland_(album)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

Mícheál Ó Domhnaill co-founded the popular Irish traditional group [The Bothy Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bothy_Band "The Bothy Band") in 1974, along with [Paddy Glackin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddy_Glackin "Paddy Glackin") (fiddle), [Matt Molloy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Molloy "Matt Molloy") (flute and tin whistle), [Paddy Keenan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddy_Keenan "Paddy Keenan") ([uilleann pipes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uilleann_pipes "Uilleann pipes") and tin whistle), [Dónal Lunny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%B3nal_Lunny "Dónal Lunny") (bouzouki, guitar, and production), and his sister [Tríona Ní Dhomhnaill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tr%C3%ADona_N%C3%AD_Dhomhnaill "Tríona Ní Dhomhnaill") ([harpsichord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpsichord "Harpsichord"), [clavinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clavinet "Clavinet") and vocals). Ó Domhnaill met [Kevin Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician) "Kevin Burke (musician)") when Burke replaced Glackin in the Bothy Band in May 1976. In the five years the Bothy Band were together, they emerged as one of the most exciting groups in the history of [Irish traditional music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music_of_Ireland "Folk music of Ireland"). Much of their repertoire was rooted in the traditional music of Ireland, and their enthusiasm and musical virtuosity set a standard for future Irish traditional performers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-harris-2) They recorded three studio albums during their brief career: _The Bothy Band_ (1975), _Old Hag You Have Killed Me_ (1976), and _Out of the Wind – Into the Sun_ (1977). A live album _After Hours_ was released in 1979, the year the group disbanded.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-harris-2)

When the Bothy Band disbanded in 1979, Burke and Ó Domhnaill toured the United Kingdom and Europe together, and recorded a highly acclaimed album, _[Promenade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promenade\_(1979\_album) "Promenade (1979 album)")_ (1979).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-harris-2) In 1980, Burke and Ó Domhnaill moved to the United States and toured extensively throughout the country.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-harris-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-tg4-doc-1-3) After settling in Portland, Oregon, the two recorded this second and final album together in 1982.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-tg4-doc-1-3) They continued to perform together the following year, but eventually parted ways to pursue other musical opportunities. Ó Domhnaill went on to form the popular group [Nightnoise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nightnoise "Nightnoise") with his sister [Tríona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tr%C3%ADona_N%C3%AD_Dhomhnaill "Tríona Ní Dhomhnaill"), [Billy Oskay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Oskay "Billy Oskay"), and Brian Dunning; he lived in Portland until 1997, when he returned to Ireland. He passed away on July 7, 2006. In addition to his acclaimed solo albums, Burke went on to form the influential Celtic groups Patrick Street and the [Celtic Fiddle Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtic_Fiddle_Festival "Celtic Fiddle Festival"), as well as successful collaborations with [Jackie Daly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Daly "Jackie Daly") and Cal Scott.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-wmc-4) Burke still lives in Portland and continues to tour throughout the world.

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Portland_(album)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Production")]

_Portland_ was recorded in Portland, Oregon in 1982.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-oregan-5) The instrumentation is restricted to Burke on fiddle, and Ó Domhnaill on vocals, guitar, and harmonium.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6)

## Composition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Portland_(album)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Composition")]

_Portland_ consists of nine tracks, five of which are medleys. The first track consists of three [reels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reel_(dance) "Reel (dance)"): "Maudabawn Chapel", was written by Ed Reavy, was learned from Martin Byrnes; "The Wild Irishman" was learned from Michael Coleman, and "The Moher Reel" was learned from Lucy Farr.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6) "Éirigh A Shiúir" is a traditional song that Ó Domhnaill learned from his aunt Neilí, a renowned singer who had a vast repertoire of Irish and English songs.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-oregan-5) The song is bout a shepherd who invites his true love to elope with him.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6) "Breton Gavottes" consists of three dances, the first and third of which are traditional, the second was written by Padrig Sicard.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6) The fourth track consists of three traditional tunes: "The Rolling Waves", "The Market Town", and "Scatter the Mud"—the latter two were learned through _O'Neill's Music of Ireland_ (1903), compiled by [Francis O'Neill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_O'Neill "Francis O'Neill"), an Irish-born American police officer and collector of Irish traditional music.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6) "Aird Uí Chumhaing" is another traditional Irish song that Ó Domhnaill learned from father, Aodh Ó Domhnaill, a teacher, a singer, and a collector of traditional music for the Irish Folklore Commission. The title refers to a townland on the northeast coast of Ireland. The song is about an exile from Aird Uí Chumhaing who looks across at his native coastline from the Mull of Kintre in Scotland and dreams of finding a boat that will carry him back to his childhood home, where he longs to live out the rest of his days.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6)

The sixth track is another medley of reels: "Paddy's Return" learned from the [Tulla Céilí Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tulla_C%C3%A9il%C3%AD_Band "The Tulla Céilí Band"), "Willy Coleman's", written by Willy Coleman who came from [County Sligo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Sligo "County Sligo"), and "Up in the Air", written by Burke and Ó Domhnaill.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6) The seventh track also consists of three reels: "Lucy's Fling" was written by Lucy Farr, "S'iomadh Rud A Chunnaic Mi", a piece of mouth music in Scottish Gaelic, was learned from Finlay MacNeill, and "Some Say the Devil is Dead", a traditional tune.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6) "Is Fada Liom Uaim Í" is another traditional song that Ó Domhnaill learned from his aunt Neilí. The song is about a man who complains that the woman he desires is beyond his reach.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6) The album's ninth and final track is a medley of four tunes: "Tom Morrison's" was written by Tom Morrison, "The Beare Island Reel" was learned from Dale Russ, "George White's Favourite" was learned from Paddy Killoran, and "Dipping the Sheep" was learned from _O'Neill's Music of Ireland_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-liner-notes-6)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Portland_(album)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Reception")]

| [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") | ![Image 5: Star](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/20px-Star_full.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)![Image 6: Star](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/20px-Star_full.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)![Image 7: Star](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/20px-Star_full.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)![Image 8: Star](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/20px-Star_full.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)![Image 9: Half star](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Star_half.svg/20px-Star_half.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-allmusic-review-7) |

Ó Domhnaill and Burke have been called "one of the finest duets ever recorded in Irish traditional music".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-hitchner-8) In contrast to the "propulsive power and bracing brinkmanship" produced by the Bothy Band, the duo set off on a different musical path that one reviewer from the _Irish Echo_ called "soulful finesse".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-hitchner-8)

> Their sound was unrushed, detailed, spellbindingly beautiful, yet still pulsing with vitality. For tunes, it was the ultimate rhythmic glide, smooth rather than slick, without a hint of coasting. For songs, it was respect and reflection conveyed with absolute conviction.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-hitchner-8)

Ó Domhnaill's guitar playing and Burke's Sligo-style Irish fiddling achieved a "relaxed vitality" through "compelling melodies, pulsing Sligo rhythms, intricate variations, and vocal perfection".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-linnet-9) Reviewers singled out the "tender, baring passion" of Ó Domhnaill's voice in his renditions of "Eirigh a Shiuir" and "Aird Ui Chumhaing".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-hitchner-8)

> He treated traditional songs in Irish as the enduring testament of history handed down by those who experienced it rather than merely documented it. His acoustic guitar playing was, like himself, unobtrusive yet intense, focused on gimmick-free impact and ever-mindful that it must support, not supplant, Burke's melodic fiddling.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-hitchner-8)

In his review for AllMusic, Steve Winick called the album "another fine display" by Burke and Ó Domhnaill, giving the album four and a half out of five stars.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_(album)#cite_note-allmusic-review-7)

Musical artist

**Kevin Burke** (born 1950) is an Irish master [fiddler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiddle "Fiddle") considered one of the finest living Irish fiddlers.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-wmc-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-mayo-news-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-fiddling-3) For nearly five decades he has been at the forefront of Irish traditional music and Celtic music,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-ceolas-4) performing and recording with the groups [The Bothy Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bothy_Band "The Bothy Band"), [Patrick Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Street "Patrick Street"), and the Celtic Fiddle Festival.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-wmc-1) He is a 2002 recipient of a [National Heritage Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Heritage_Fellowship "National Heritage Fellowship") from the [National Endowment for the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Endowment_for_the_Arts "National Endowment for the Arts").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-mayo-news-2)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-nea-5) He is also regarded as a [fiddle-singing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiddle-singing "Fiddle-singing") pioneer.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-6)

In addition to his solo albums, Burke has had successful project collaborations with [Christy Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christy_Moore "Christy Moore"), [Andy Irvine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Irvine_(musician) "Andy Irvine (musician)")&[Paul Brady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Brady "Paul Brady"), [Mícheál Ó Domhnaill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%ADche%C3%A1l_%C3%93_Domhnaill "Mícheál Ó Domhnaill"), [Jackie Daly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Daly "Jackie Daly"), Ged Foley and Cal Scott.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-wmc-1)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kevin_Burke_(musician)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Kevin Burke was born in 1950 in London, England to parents from [County Sligo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Sligo "County Sligo") in Ireland.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-harris-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-8) Inheriting a love of Irish music from his parents, he took up the fiddle at the age of eight, studied under Jessie Christopherson,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-kb-bio-beginning-9) and eventually developed an advanced technique in the [Sligo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sligo "Sligo") fiddling style. He travelled frequently to Ireland to visit relatives and immersed himself in the local Sligo music.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-10) By the age of thirteen, he was playing with Irish musical groups.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-nea-5)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kevin_Burke_(musician)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Burke joined a [céilí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9ilidh "Céilidh") band, the Glenside, and played weekends at various Irish dance halls around London. In 1966, the Glenside performed at the céilí band competition at the All-Ireland Fleadh in Boyle in [County Roscommon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Roscommon "County Roscommon") and won the competition.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-kb-bio-youth-11)

In 1972, Burke met American singer-songwriter [Arlo Guthrie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlo_Guthrie "Arlo Guthrie") in a pub in [Milltown Malbay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milltown_Malbay "Milltown Malbay") in [County Clare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Clare "County Clare"). Impressed with Burke's fiddling, Guthrie invited him to Los Angeles to play on his album _[Last of the Brooklyn Cowboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last\_of\_the\_Brooklyn\_Cowboys "Last of the Brooklyn Cowboys")_ (1973).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-nea-5) Burke's exposure to the musicians he met in the United States—including accordionist Joe Burke and fiddler Andy McGann—inspired him to make a career of playing music.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-kb-bio-stage-12) In 1974, Burke moved to [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin"), where he teamed up with singer-songwriter [Christy Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christy_Moore "Christy Moore"), a former member of the Irish band [Planxty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planxty "Planxty").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-harris-7) Together with Jimmy Faulkner and Declan McNelis, they played throughout Ireland for the next few years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-kb-bio-stage-12)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/Kevin_Burke_1.jpg/250px-Kevin_Burke_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kevin_Burke_1.jpg)

Burke at the [Dublin Irish Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin_Irish_Festival "Dublin Irish Festival"), 2008

In 1976, Burke became a member of the Irish traditional music group [The Bothy Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bothy_Band "The Bothy Band"); the band, active for three years in the late 1970s, was well-known for its enthusiastic and highly skilled performances.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-allmusic-bothy-13) Burke replaced [Tommy Peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Peoples "Tommy Peoples") on fiddle, and soon became an integral member of the group, appearing on three of their albums: _Old Hag You Have Killed Me_ (1976), _Out of the Wind – Into the Sun_ (1977), and _After Hours (Live in Paris)_ (1979).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-harris-7)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-WaltersMansfield1998-14) Burke developed a friendship with the band's guitarist and vocalist, [Mícheál Ó Domhnaill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%ADche%C3%A1l_%C3%93_Domhnaill "Mícheál Ó Domhnaill"), and soon the two began appearing together as a duo. When the Bothy Band disbanded in 1979, they toured the United Kingdom and Europe together, and recorded the album _[Promenade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promenade\_(1979\_album) "Promenade (1979 album)")_ (1979).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-harris-7) In 1980, Burke and Ó Domhnaill moved to the United States[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-15) and toured throughout the country before settling in [Portland, Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland,_Oregon "Portland, Oregon"), where they recorded a second album, _[Portland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland\_(album) "Portland (album)")_ (1982).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-harris-7)

In 1985, Burke joined the Legends of Irish Music tour, where he played with Irish musicians [Andy Irvine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Irvine_(musician) "Andy Irvine (musician)") (vocals, bouzouki, mandolin and harmonica) and [Jackie Daly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Daly "Jackie Daly") (accordion).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-FR66-16):34–35[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-Irvine8-17) Together they formed the group Patrick Street.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-harris-7) During the next two decades, the group released nine albums (excluding two compilations): _[Patrick Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick\_Street\_(album) "Patrick Street (album)")_ (1987), _[No. 2 Patrick Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No.\_2\_Patrick\_Street "No. 2 Patrick Street")_ (1988), _[Irish Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish\_Times\_(album) "Irish Times (album)")_ (1990), _[All in Good Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All\_in\_Good\_Time\_(Patrick\_Street\_album) "All in Good Time (Patrick Street album)")_ (1993), _[Cornerboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornerboys "Cornerboys")_ (1996), _[Made in Cork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Made\_in\_Cork "Made in Cork")_ (1997), _[Live from Patrick Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live\_from\_Patrick\_Street "Live from Patrick Street")_ (1999), _[Street Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street\_Life\_(Patrick\_Street\_album) "Street Life (Patrick Street album)")_ (2002), and _[On the Fly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_the\_Fly\_(album) "On the Fly (album)")_ (2007).

In 1992, Burke recorded the solo album _Open House_ with Mark Graham (harmonica, clarinet, vocals), Paul Kotapish (guitar, mandolin, cittern, bass), and [Sandy Silva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandy_Silva?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sandy Silva (page does not exist)") (percussive dance).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-harris-7) These three comprised the core of his band and together, as the group Open House, they recorded two other albums, _Second Story_ (1994) and _Hoof and Mouth_ (1997). In the early 1990s, Burke started touring and recording with Scottish fiddler [Johnny Cunningham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Cunningham "Johnny Cunningham") and Breton fiddler Christian Lemaître as the [Celtic Fiddle Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtic_Fiddle_Festival "Celtic Fiddle Festival").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-18) Together they released six albums: _Celtic Fiddle Festival_ (1993),[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-19)_Celtic Fiddle Festival: Encore_ (1998), _Rendezvous_ (2001), _Play On_ (2005), _Equinoxe_ (2008), and _Live in Brittany_ (2013).

In 2002, Burke was awarded a [National Heritage Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Heritage_Fellowship "National Heritage Fellowship") from the [National Endowment for the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Endowment_for_the_Arts "National Endowment for the Arts"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-nea-5) the highest honour given in the United States for folk and traditional arts.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-mayo-news-2) In recent years, Burke partnered with Ged Foley to record _In Tandem_ (2006), and collaborated with documentary film composer Cal Scott on the album _Across the Black River_ (2007) and follow-up album _Suite_ (2010). In 2007, Burke started an independent record company, Loftus Music, to release his own recordings. Burke continues to tour throughout the world, including performances in Australia in 2013.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-20)

In 2016, Burke was awarded the "Gradam Ceoil" (Musician of the Year) in the traditional-music awards presented by the Irish-language TV channel [TG4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TG4 "TG4").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-gradam-21)

He currently lives in Portland, Oregon with his wife and two children.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-carey-22)

## Playing style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kevin_Burke_(musician)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Playing style")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Kevin_Burke_4.jpg/250px-Kevin_Burke_4.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kevin_Burke_4.jpg)

Burke at The Abbey in [Nicholls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholls,_Australian_Capital_Territory "Nicholls, Australian Capital Territory"), Australia, 2014

Burke's fiddle playing style was heavily influenced by the Sligo style playing of Michael Coleman, Paddy Killoran, and James Morrison.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-fiddling-3) Burke described the style as being "the best of both worlds"—combining the driving rhythm of Donegal style and the smooth lyricism of Clare style.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-fiddling-3) While acknowledging that his playing is "based on" the Sligo style, he also acknowledges being influenced by many different musical styles outside of Irish traditional music. For example, one of the distinctive features of his playing is the "strong backbeat he applies to many reels, with emphasis on every third quaver", presenting the emphasised beat with an up bow, versus the traditional approach of playing that pattern with an emphasised downbow.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-fiddling-3) Burke also emphasises the strong beat by playing "an adjacent open string as the bow digs in".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-fiddling-3)

## Instruments and equipment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kevin_Burke_(musician)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Instruments and equipment")]

Burke currently plays a [fiddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiddle "Fiddle") made by Michiel De Hoog, a Dutch violin maker working in Dublin. In 2000, his old Tony Martin fiddle had become unstable, despite several repair attempts. Looking for a more stable instrument to play on the road, he turned to his friend De Hoog, who had just finished an instrument. After playing it in the shop, Burke purchased it and has been playing it almost exclusively since. Occasionally, he will play his old Tony Martin fiddle or a fiddle made by Jeff Manthos of Oregon.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-kb-tools-23)

Burke uses Obligato strings made by Pirastro and [rosin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosin "Rosin") made by Gustave Bernadel. The bow he uses exclusively was given to him by his brother Noel Burke, a [bow maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow_maker "Bow maker"), in 2000 for his fiftieth birthday. He carries his fiddle and gear in a Maurizio Riboni case from Cremona, Italy.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-kb-tools-23) To amplify his instrument, Burke uses an MBC-603 [condenser microphone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condenser_microphone "Condenser microphone") on a stand. Sometimes he uses a Swiss-made Kurmann Soundpost pick-up designed by Ronnie Arber Audiotechnik along with the microphone.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-kb-tools-23)

Musical artist

**Kevin Burke** (born 1950) is an Irish master [fiddler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiddle "Fiddle") considered one of the finest living Irish fiddlers.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-wmc-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-mayo-news-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-fiddling-3) For nearly five decades he has been at the forefront of Irish traditional music and Celtic music,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-ceolas-4) performing and recording with the groups [The Bothy Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bothy_Band "The Bothy Band"), [Patrick Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Street "Patrick Street"), and the Celtic Fiddle Festival.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-wmc-1) He is a 2002 recipient of a [National Heritage Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Heritage_Fellowship "National Heritage Fellowship") from the [National Endowment for the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Endowment_for_the_Arts "National Endowment for the Arts").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-mayo-news-2)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-nea-5) He is also regarded as a [fiddle-singing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiddle-singing "Fiddle-singing") pioneer.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-6)

In addition to his solo albums, Burke has had successful project collaborations with [Christy Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christy_Moore "Christy Moore"), [Andy Irvine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Irvine_(musician) "Andy Irvine (musician)")&[Paul Brady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Brady "Paul Brady"), [Mícheál Ó Domhnaill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%ADche%C3%A1l_%C3%93_Domhnaill "Mícheál Ó Domhnaill"), [Jackie Daly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Daly "Jackie Daly"), Ged Foley and Cal Scott.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-wmc-1)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kevin_Burke_(musician)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Kevin Burke was born in 1950 in London, England to parents from [County Sligo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Sligo "County Sligo") in Ireland.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-harris-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-8) Inheriting a love of Irish music from his parents, he took up the fiddle at the age of eight, studied under Jessie Christopherson,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-kb-bio-beginning-9) and eventually developed an advanced technique in the [Sligo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sligo "Sligo") fiddling style. He travelled frequently to Ireland to visit relatives and immersed himself in the local Sligo music.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-10) By the age of thirteen, he was playing with Irish musical groups.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-nea-5)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kevin_Burke_(musician)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Burke joined a [céilí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9ilidh "Céilidh") band, the Glenside, and played weekends at various Irish dance halls around London. In 1966, the Glenside performed at the céilí band competition at the All-Ireland Fleadh in Boyle in [County Roscommon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Roscommon "County Roscommon") and won the competition.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-kb-bio-youth-11)

In 1972, Burke met American singer-songwriter [Arlo Guthrie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlo_Guthrie "Arlo Guthrie") in a pub in [Milltown Malbay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milltown_Malbay "Milltown Malbay") in [County Clare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Clare "County Clare"). Impressed with Burke's fiddling, Guthrie invited him to Los Angeles to play on his album _[Last of the Brooklyn Cowboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last\_of\_the\_Brooklyn\_Cowboys "Last of the Brooklyn Cowboys")_ (1973).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-nea-5) Burke's exposure to the musicians he met in the United States—including accordionist Joe Burke and fiddler Andy McGann—inspired him to make a career of playing music.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-kb-bio-stage-12) In 1974, Burke moved to [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin"), where he teamed up with singer-songwriter [Christy Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christy_Moore "Christy Moore"), a former member of the Irish band [Planxty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planxty "Planxty").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-harris-7) Together with Jimmy Faulkner and Declan McNelis, they played throughout Ireland for the next few years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-kb-bio-stage-12)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/Kevin_Burke_1.jpg/250px-Kevin_Burke_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kevin_Burke_1.jpg)

Burke at the [Dublin Irish Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin_Irish_Festival "Dublin Irish Festival"), 2008

In 1976, Burke became a member of the Irish traditional music group [The Bothy Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bothy_Band "The Bothy Band"); the band, active for three years in the late 1970s, was well-known for its enthusiastic and highly skilled performances.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-allmusic-bothy-13) Burke replaced [Tommy Peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Peoples "Tommy Peoples") on fiddle, and soon became an integral member of the group, appearing on three of their albums: _Old Hag You Have Killed Me_ (1976), _Out of the Wind – Into the Sun_ (1977), and _After Hours (Live in Paris)_ (1979).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-harris-7)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-WaltersMansfield1998-14) Burke developed a friendship with the band's guitarist and vocalist, [Mícheál Ó Domhnaill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%ADche%C3%A1l_%C3%93_Domhnaill "Mícheál Ó Domhnaill"), and soon the two began appearing together as a duo. When the Bothy Band disbanded in 1979, they toured the United Kingdom and Europe together, and recorded the album _[Promenade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promenade\_(1979\_album) "Promenade (1979 album)")_ (1979).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-harris-7) In 1980, Burke and Ó Domhnaill moved to the United States[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-15) and toured throughout the country before settling in [Portland, Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland,_Oregon "Portland, Oregon"), where they recorded a second album, _[Portland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland\_(album) "Portland (album)")_ (1982).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-harris-7)

In 1985, Burke joined the Legends of Irish Music tour, where he played with Irish musicians [Andy Irvine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Irvine_(musician) "Andy Irvine (musician)") (vocals, bouzouki, mandolin and harmonica) and [Jackie Daly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Daly "Jackie Daly") (accordion).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-FR66-16):34–35[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-Irvine8-17) Together they formed the group Patrick Street.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-harris-7) During the next two decades, the group released nine albums (excluding two compilations): _[Patrick Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick\_Street\_(album) "Patrick Street (album)")_ (1987), _[No. 2 Patrick Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No.\_2\_Patrick\_Street "No. 2 Patrick Street")_ (1988), _[Irish Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish\_Times\_(album) "Irish Times (album)")_ (1990), _[All in Good Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All\_in\_Good\_Time\_(Patrick\_Street\_album) "All in Good Time (Patrick Street album)")_ (1993), _[Cornerboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornerboys "Cornerboys")_ (1996), _[Made in Cork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Made\_in\_Cork "Made in Cork")_ (1997), _[Live from Patrick Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live\_from\_Patrick\_Street "Live from Patrick Street")_ (1999), _[Street Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street\_Life\_(Patrick\_Street\_album) "Street Life (Patrick Street album)")_ (2002), and _[On the Fly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_the\_Fly\_(album) "On the Fly (album)")_ (2007).

In 1992, Burke recorded the solo album _Open House_ with Mark Graham (harmonica, clarinet, vocals), Paul Kotapish (guitar, mandolin, cittern, bass), and [Sandy Silva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandy_Silva?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sandy Silva (page does not exist)") (percussive dance).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-harris-7) These three comprised the core of his band and together, as the group Open House, they recorded two other albums, _Second Story_ (1994) and _Hoof and Mouth_ (1997). In the early 1990s, Burke started touring and recording with Scottish fiddler [Johnny Cunningham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Cunningham "Johnny Cunningham") and Breton fiddler Christian Lemaître as the [Celtic Fiddle Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtic_Fiddle_Festival "Celtic Fiddle Festival").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-18) Together they released six albums: _Celtic Fiddle Festival_ (1993),[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-19)_Celtic Fiddle Festival: Encore_ (1998), _Rendezvous_ (2001), _Play On_ (2005), _Equinoxe_ (2008), and _Live in Brittany_ (2013).

In 2002, Burke was awarded a [National Heritage Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Heritage_Fellowship "National Heritage Fellowship") from the [National Endowment for the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Endowment_for_the_Arts "National Endowment for the Arts"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-nea-5) the highest honour given in the United States for folk and traditional arts.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-mayo-news-2) In recent years, Burke partnered with Ged Foley to record _In Tandem_ (2006), and collaborated with documentary film composer Cal Scott on the album _Across the Black River_ (2007) and follow-up album _Suite_ (2010). In 2007, Burke started an independent record company, Loftus Music, to release his own recordings. Burke continues to tour throughout the world, including performances in Australia in 2013.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-20)

In 2016, Burke was awarded the "Gradam Ceoil" (Musician of the Year) in the traditional-music awards presented by the Irish-language TV channel [TG4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TG4 "TG4").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-gradam-21)

He currently lives in Portland, Oregon with his wife and two children.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-carey-22)

## Playing style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kevin_Burke_(musician)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Playing style")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Kevin_Burke_4.jpg/250px-Kevin_Burke_4.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kevin_Burke_4.jpg)

Burke at The Abbey in [Nicholls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholls,_Australian_Capital_Territory "Nicholls, Australian Capital Territory"), Australia, 2014

Burke's fiddle playing style was heavily influenced by the Sligo style playing of Michael Coleman, Paddy Killoran, and James Morrison.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-fiddling-3) Burke described the style as being "the best of both worlds"—combining the driving rhythm of Donegal style and the smooth lyricism of Clare style.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-fiddling-3) While acknowledging that his playing is "based on" the Sligo style, he also acknowledges being influenced by many different musical styles outside of Irish traditional music. For example, one of the distinctive features of his playing is the "strong backbeat he applies to many reels, with emphasis on every third quaver", presenting the emphasised beat with an up bow, versus the traditional approach of playing that pattern with an emphasised downbow.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-fiddling-3) Burke also emphasises the strong beat by playing "an adjacent open string as the bow digs in".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-fiddling-3)

## Instruments and equipment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kevin_Burke_(musician)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Instruments and equipment")]

Burke currently plays a [fiddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiddle "Fiddle") made by Michiel De Hoog, a Dutch violin maker working in Dublin. In 2000, his old Tony Martin fiddle had become unstable, despite several repair attempts. Looking for a more stable instrument to play on the road, he turned to his friend De Hoog, who had just finished an instrument. After playing it in the shop, Burke purchased it and has been playing it almost exclusively since. Occasionally, he will play his old Tony Martin fiddle or a fiddle made by Jeff Manthos of Oregon.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-kb-tools-23)

Burke uses Obligato strings made by Pirastro and [rosin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosin "Rosin") made by Gustave Bernadel. The bow he uses exclusively was given to him by his brother Noel Burke, a [bow maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow_maker "Bow maker"), in 2000 for his fiftieth birthday. He carries his fiddle and gear in a Maurizio Riboni case from Cremona, Italy.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-kb-tools-23) To amplify his instrument, Burke uses an MBC-603 [condenser microphone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condenser_microphone "Condenser microphone") on a stand. Sometimes he uses a Swiss-made Kurmann Soundpost pick-up designed by Ronnie Arber Audiotechnik along with the microphone.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Burke_(musician)#cite_note-kb-tools-23)

**Hometown**, **HomeTown**, or **Home Town** may refer to:

*   A hometown, the town where someone lives or the town that they come from, typically their [place of birth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_of_birth "Place of birth").
*   In developing nations particularly: [native place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_place "Native place"), village of origin in newly urbanized societies.

_**Austin**_ is the fifth studio album by American musician [Post Malone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone "Post Malone"). It was released through [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_Records "Mercury Records") and [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records") on July 28, 2023. The bonus version of the album was released five days later to include a new track. Production was handled by Malone himself, [Andrew Watt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Watt_(record_producer) "Andrew Watt (record producer)"), [Louis Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Bell "Louis Bell"), [Max Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Martin "Max Martin"), and [Rami Yacoub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rami_Yacoub "Rami Yacoub"). _Austin_ was supported by four singles: "[Chemical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_(Post_Malone_song) "Chemical (Post Malone song)")", "[Mourning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourning_(Post_Malone_song) "Mourning (Post Malone song)")", "[Overdrive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdrive_(Post_Malone_song) "Overdrive (Post Malone song)")", and "[Enough Is Enough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enough_Is_Enough_(Post_Malone_song) "Enough Is Enough (Post Malone song)")". A departure from the [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop") and [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_R&B "Contemporary R&B")-influenced sounds of its predecessors, it is a guitar-based [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music"), [indie pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_pop "Indie pop"), and [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock") album, and is Malone's first and only project not to feature any [guest appearances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guest_appearance "Guest appearance").

_Austin_ received generally positive reviews from [music critics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_journalism "Music journalism") and debuted at number two on [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart, in which it earned 113,000 [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_unit "Album-equivalent unit"), of which 34,000 units were pure album sales.

## Background and promotion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Austin_(album)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and promotion")]

On May 15, 2023, Malone posted a video on [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram "Instagram") to announce the album, which is titled after his real first name.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-5) The message hinted at a different artistic approach, possibly intensifying the sound of his fourth studio album, _[Twelve Carat Toothache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve\_Carat\_Toothache "Twelve Carat Toothache")_ (2022).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-6) Malone revealed that he played the guitar on every single song on the album, calling the creation process a "fun experience".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-7) He described the outcome as the "most challenging and rewarding music" he had ever made, which was a product of constantly making himself work to make it.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-8) That same day, Malone also announced a summer North American tour called the [If Y'all Weren't Here, I'd Be Crying Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_Y'all_Weren't_Here,_I'd_Be_Crying_Tour "If Y'all Weren't Here, I'd Be Crying Tour") to accompany the release of the album, which later became a world tour that started on July 8 and ended on December 3, 2023.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-9)

### Singles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Austin_(album)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Singles")]

On April 14, 2023, Malone released the lead single of the album, "[Chemical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_(Post_Malone_song) "Chemical (Post Malone song)")".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-10) The second single of the album, "[Mourning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourning_(Post_Malone_song) "Mourning (Post Malone song)")", was released on May 19.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-11) The third single, "[Overdrive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdrive_(Post_Malone_song) "Overdrive (Post Malone song)")", was released on July 14.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-12) The fourth and final single, "[Enough Is Enough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enough_Is_Enough_(Post_Malone_song) "Enough Is Enough (Post Malone song)")", was sent to Italian [contemporary hit radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_hit_radio "Contemporary hit radio"), on September 8, 2023.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-13)

_Austin_ was met with generally positive reviews. At [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which assigns a rating out of 100 to reviews from professional publications, the album received a [weighted average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_arithmetic_mean "Weighted arithmetic mean") score of 66, based on 10 reviews, indicating "generally favorable reviews".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-MC-15) Aggregator AnyDecentMusic? gave it 5.5 out of 10, based on their assessment of the critical consensus.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-ADM-14)

Neil Z. Yeung of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") praised the album, stating, "Melodic and heartfelt, _Austin_ surprises at nearly every turn, whether that's by an unexpected sonic detour or the simple fact that Post Malone has never sounded this fearless".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-AllMusic-16) Erica Campbell of _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_ wrote that Malone's "shift from [trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trap_music "Trap music") beats and [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop") delivery to purer [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") suits [him] well, proving that slowing down can be a creative advantage, especially when you're heading in the right direction",[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-NME-19) while _[Clash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash\_(magazine) "Clash (magazine)")_'s Robin Murray described _Austin_ as "an album that dares to buck trends, and at its best can be genuinely moving".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-Clash-18)_[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ critic Chris Willman said, "It sounds like sobering stuff on paper. But on record, a lot of these songs play out as breezily as [Styles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Styles "Harry Styles")' "[As It Was](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/As_It_Was "As It Was")". It's a record that's in constant conflict with itself, using candor and humor as a self-conscious form of denial, maybe; the easygoing infectiousness of the music always is reassuring us that there's nothing to worry about amid all this conspicuous consumption".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-24) Reviewing the album for _[American Songwriter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Songwriter "American Songwriter")_, Thomas Galindo stated, "While his 17 new songs don't amount to a flawless masterpiece, they do paint a picture of a Post Malone who not only knows he needs to turn things around, but also intends to at any cost".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-AS-17)

_[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_'s Clayton Purdom wrote that "even if _Austin_ is Post's guitar record, it's not his [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") record", and found that "plenty of it works" even if "the immense self-loathing with which the record introduces itself finds no clear resolution by the end, despite many allusions on otherwise-peppy songs".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-25) Paul Attard of _[Slant Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slant\_Magazine "Slant Magazine")_ commented that "little on the album could be regarded as hip-hop-oriented" as its tracks "are primarily structured around stadium-sized pop hooks", which he found "all follow the same overly simplistic pop structure".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-Slant-22) Writing for _[Pitchfork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork\_(website) "Pitchfork (website)")_, Brad Shoup felt that _Austin_ "is Post at his strongest: audaciously raiding the entire pop toolkit" and "even after forsaking Los Angeles for Utah, his life remains a movie: loaded with state-of-the-industry pyrotechnics, bristling with guns, and littered with synergistic product tie-ins", which makes the album "in directorial terms, a one-for-me situation: a passion project secured with almost a decade at the summit of [pop rap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rap "Pop rap") as collateral".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-Pitchfork-21)_Riff Magazine_ wrote that _Austin_ was "influenced by '80s and '90s [alternative rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock")," which tended to "slow down the middle of the album."[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-Simons-26)

## Commercial performance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Austin_(album)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Commercial performance")]

In the United States, _Austin_ debuted at number two on [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart, earning 113,000 [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_unit "Album-equivalent unit") (including 34,000 in pure album sales) in its first week. This became Malone's fifth top-five album on the chart after all his previous studio albums reached the top five. The album also accumulated a total of 101.14 million on-demand streams of the album's songs.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-27)

_**Austin**_ is the fifth studio album by American musician [Post Malone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone "Post Malone"). It was released through [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_Records "Mercury Records") and [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records") on July 28, 2023. The bonus version of the album was released five days later to include a new track. Production was handled by Malone himself, [Andrew Watt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Watt_(record_producer) "Andrew Watt (record producer)"), [Louis Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Bell "Louis Bell"), [Max Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Martin "Max Martin"), and [Rami Yacoub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rami_Yacoub "Rami Yacoub"). _Austin_ was supported by four singles: "[Chemical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_(Post_Malone_song) "Chemical (Post Malone song)")", "[Mourning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourning_(Post_Malone_song) "Mourning (Post Malone song)")", "[Overdrive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdrive_(Post_Malone_song) "Overdrive (Post Malone song)")", and "[Enough Is Enough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enough_Is_Enough_(Post_Malone_song) "Enough Is Enough (Post Malone song)")". A departure from the [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop") and [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_R&B "Contemporary R&B")-influenced sounds of its predecessors, it is a guitar-based [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music"), [indie pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_pop "Indie pop"), and [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock") album, and is Malone's first and only project not to feature any [guest appearances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guest_appearance "Guest appearance").

_Austin_ received generally positive reviews from [music critics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_journalism "Music journalism") and debuted at number two on [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart, in which it earned 113,000 [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_unit "Album-equivalent unit"), of which 34,000 units were pure album sales.

## Background and promotion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Austin_(album)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and promotion")]

On May 15, 2023, Malone posted a video on [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram "Instagram") to announce the album, which is titled after his real first name.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-5) The message hinted at a different artistic approach, possibly intensifying the sound of his fourth studio album, _[Twelve Carat Toothache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve\_Carat\_Toothache "Twelve Carat Toothache")_ (2022).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-6) Malone revealed that he played the guitar on every single song on the album, calling the creation process a "fun experience".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-7) He described the outcome as the "most challenging and rewarding music" he had ever made, which was a product of constantly making himself work to make it.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-8) That same day, Malone also announced a summer North American tour called the [If Y'all Weren't Here, I'd Be Crying Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_Y'all_Weren't_Here,_I'd_Be_Crying_Tour "If Y'all Weren't Here, I'd Be Crying Tour") to accompany the release of the album, which later became a world tour that started on July 8 and ended on December 3, 2023.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-9)

### Singles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Austin_(album)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Singles")]

On April 14, 2023, Malone released the lead single of the album, "[Chemical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_(Post_Malone_song) "Chemical (Post Malone song)")".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-10) The second single of the album, "[Mourning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourning_(Post_Malone_song) "Mourning (Post Malone song)")", was released on May 19.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-11) The third single, "[Overdrive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdrive_(Post_Malone_song) "Overdrive (Post Malone song)")", was released on July 14.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-12) The fourth and final single, "[Enough Is Enough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enough_Is_Enough_(Post_Malone_song) "Enough Is Enough (Post Malone song)")", was sent to Italian [contemporary hit radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_hit_radio "Contemporary hit radio"), on September 8, 2023.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-13)

_Austin_ was met with generally positive reviews. At [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which assigns a rating out of 100 to reviews from professional publications, the album received a [weighted average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_arithmetic_mean "Weighted arithmetic mean") score of 66, based on 10 reviews, indicating "generally favorable reviews".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-MC-15) Aggregator AnyDecentMusic? gave it 5.5 out of 10, based on their assessment of the critical consensus.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-ADM-14)

Neil Z. Yeung of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") praised the album, stating, "Melodic and heartfelt, _Austin_ surprises at nearly every turn, whether that's by an unexpected sonic detour or the simple fact that Post Malone has never sounded this fearless".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-AllMusic-16) Erica Campbell of _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_ wrote that Malone's "shift from [trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trap_music "Trap music") beats and [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop") delivery to purer [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") suits [him] well, proving that slowing down can be a creative advantage, especially when you're heading in the right direction",[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-NME-19) while _[Clash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash\_(magazine) "Clash (magazine)")_'s Robin Murray described _Austin_ as "an album that dares to buck trends, and at its best can be genuinely moving".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-Clash-18)_[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ critic Chris Willman said, "It sounds like sobering stuff on paper. But on record, a lot of these songs play out as breezily as [Styles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Styles "Harry Styles")' "[As It Was](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/As_It_Was "As It Was")". It's a record that's in constant conflict with itself, using candor and humor as a self-conscious form of denial, maybe; the easygoing infectiousness of the music always is reassuring us that there's nothing to worry about amid all this conspicuous consumption".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-24) Reviewing the album for _[American Songwriter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Songwriter "American Songwriter")_, Thomas Galindo stated, "While his 17 new songs don't amount to a flawless masterpiece, they do paint a picture of a Post Malone who not only knows he needs to turn things around, but also intends to at any cost".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-AS-17)

_[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_'s Clayton Purdom wrote that "even if _Austin_ is Post's guitar record, it's not his [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") record", and found that "plenty of it works" even if "the immense self-loathing with which the record introduces itself finds no clear resolution by the end, despite many allusions on otherwise-peppy songs".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-25) Paul Attard of _[Slant Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slant\_Magazine "Slant Magazine")_ commented that "little on the album could be regarded as hip-hop-oriented" as its tracks "are primarily structured around stadium-sized pop hooks", which he found "all follow the same overly simplistic pop structure".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-Slant-22) Writing for _[Pitchfork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork\_(website) "Pitchfork (website)")_, Brad Shoup felt that _Austin_ "is Post at his strongest: audaciously raiding the entire pop toolkit" and "even after forsaking Los Angeles for Utah, his life remains a movie: loaded with state-of-the-industry pyrotechnics, bristling with guns, and littered with synergistic product tie-ins", which makes the album "in directorial terms, a one-for-me situation: a passion project secured with almost a decade at the summit of [pop rap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rap "Pop rap") as collateral".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-Pitchfork-21)_Riff Magazine_ wrote that _Austin_ was "influenced by '80s and '90s [alternative rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock")," which tended to "slow down the middle of the album."[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-Simons-26)

## Commercial performance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Austin_(album)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Commercial performance")]

In the United States, _Austin_ debuted at number two on [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart, earning 113,000 [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_unit "Album-equivalent unit") (including 34,000 in pure album sales) in its first week. This became Malone's fifth top-five album on the chart after all his previous studio albums reached the top five. The album also accumulated a total of 101.14 million on-demand streams of the album's songs.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album)#cite_note-27)

**Austin Richard Post** (born July 4, 1995),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-Syr-3) known professionally as **Post Malone**, is an American singer, rapper, songwriter, record producer, and actor.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-:2-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-5) His music blends various genres including [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music"), [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop"), [trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trap_music "Trap music"), [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music"), [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_R&B "Contemporary R&B"), and [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music").

Malone began his musical career in 2010, and earned mainstream recognition with his 2015 [cloud rap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_rap "Cloud rap") debut single, "[White Iverson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Iverson "White Iverson")".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-WhiteIversonSC-6) The song led him to sign with [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-Schwartz2015-7) and served as lead single for his debut studio album, _[Stoney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoney\_(album) "Stoney (album)")_ (2016), which spawned the [Diamond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification")-certified single "[Congratulations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congratulations_(Post_Malone_song) "Congratulations (Post Malone song)")" (featuring [Quavo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quavo "Quavo")). His second album, _[Beerbongs & Bentleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beerbongs\_&\_Bentleys "Beerbongs & Bentleys")_ (2018), debuted atop the US [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") and set numerous [streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media "Streaming media") records. It contained the US [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") number-one singles "[Rockstar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockstar_(Post_Malone_song) "Rockstar (Post Malone song)")" (featuring [21 Savage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21_Savage "21 Savage")) and "[Psycho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psycho_(Post_Malone_song) "Psycho (Post Malone song)")" (featuring [Ty Dolla Sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ty_Dolla_Sign "Ty Dolla Sign")), and was nominated for [Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year") at the [61st Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/61st_Annual_Grammy_Awards "61st Annual Grammy Awards"). His third Hot 100 number-one single, "[Sunflower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunflower_(Post_Malone_and_Swae_Lee_song) "Sunflower (Post Malone and Swae Lee song)")", a duet with [Swae Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swae_Lee "Swae Lee"), was released for [the accompanying soundtrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider-Man:_Into_the_Spider-Verse_(soundtrack) "Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse (soundtrack)") to the 2018 animated film _[Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider-Man:\_Into\_the\_Spider-Verse "Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse")_; it became the highest-certified song in [RIAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") history and was the first to receive a 2× Diamond certification.

Malone's third album, _[Hollywood's Bleeding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood's\_Bleeding "Hollywood's Bleeding")_ (2019), became his second project to both debut atop the _Billboard_ 200 and receive Grammy Award nomination for Album of the Year.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-8) It spawned the single "[Circles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circles_(Post_Malone_song) "Circles (Post Malone song)")", which spent 61 weeks on the Hot 100, becoming Malone's biggest hit single to date.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-9) Malone's fourth and fifth albums, _[Twelve Carat Toothache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve\_Carat\_Toothache "Twelve Carat Toothache")_ (2022) and [_Austin_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_(album) "Austin (album)") (2023), both peaked at number two on the _Billboard_ 200. In 2024, he topped the _Billboard_ Hot 100 twice more with his guest appearance on [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift")'s "[Fortnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortnight_(song) "Fortnight (song)")" and his first [country pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_pop "Country pop") song, "[I Had Some Help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Had_Some_Help "I Had Some Help")" (featuring [Morgan Wallen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Wallen "Morgan Wallen")). The latter served as the lead single for Malone's sixth album and country music debut, _[F-1 Trillion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-1\_Trillion "F-1 Trillion")_ (2024), which became his third number-one album on the _Billboard_ 200.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-10)

Malone is among the [best-selling music artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_music_artists "List of best-selling music artists"), with over 150 million records sold in the US alone according to the RIAA.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-11) His [accolades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_awards_and_nominations_received_by_Post_Malone "List of awards and nominations received by Post Malone") include eleven [_Billboard_ Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Music_Award "Billboard Music Award"), five [American Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Music_Awards "American Music Awards"), six [MTV Video Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV_Video_Music_Awards "MTV Video Music Awards"), and eighteen [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award") nominations.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-13) He holds several _Billboard_ chart records: He is the first solo lead artist to top both the [Rap Airplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rap_Airplay "Rap Airplay") and [Adult Contemporary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_Contemporary_(chart) "Adult Contemporary (chart)") charts, while "Circles" set the record for longest climb to number one (41 weeks) on the [Adult Contemporary chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_Contemporary_(chart) "Adult Contemporary (chart)") by a solo artist.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-14)As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Post_Malone&action=edit), Malone is second only to Drake for artists with the most diamond-certified songs, with nine to his name.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-15)

## Early life

Austin Richard Post was born on July 4, 1995,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-Syr-3) in [Syracuse, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syracuse,_New_York "Syracuse, New York").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-:5-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-17) He was raised by his father, Richard Post, and his stepmother, Jodie. His father had been a [DJ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disc_jockey "Disc jockey") in his youth and introduced Malone to many genres of music including [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop"), [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music"), and [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-Syr-3) When Malone was nine years old,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-18) he and his family moved to [Grapevine, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grapevine,_Texas "Grapevine, Texas"), after his father became the manager of [concessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concession_stand "Concession stand") for the [Dallas Cowboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Cowboys "Dallas Cowboys") football team.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-papermag-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-:0-20) According to Malone, his first foray into professional music began when he played guitar in a local [metalcore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metalcore "Metalcore") band.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-AlSharif2019-21) His interest in the genre persisted past this endeavor as he also auditioned as a guitarist for the Texas-based metalcore group [Crown the Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_the_Empire "Crown the Empire") in 2010, but was rejected after his guitar strings broke during the audition. He credited his initial interest in learning guitar to the video game series _[Guitar Hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar\_Hero "Guitar Hero")_.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-rollingstone-22)

Malone has expressed his affinity for [alternative rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock") music, and appeared for a DJ set at Emo Nite in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), California, in June 2017, playing songs by [My Chemical Romance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Chemical_Romance "My Chemical Romance") at the event.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-23) He says soon afterwards he transitioned to softer rock as well as hip-hop, before beginning to experiment on [FL Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FL_Studio "FL Studio").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-24)

## Career

### 2010–2016: Career beginnings, _August 26th_ and _Stoney_

Main articles: [_August 26th_ (mixtape)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_26th_(mixtape) "August 26th (mixtape)") and [_Stoney_ (album)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoney_(album) "Stoney (album)")

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Postmalone-ritual-may7-DREWYORKE-56_%2817275323379%29.jpg/250px-Postmalone-ritual-may7-DREWYORKE-56_%2817275323379%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Postmalone-ritual-may7-DREWYORKE-56_(17275323379).jpg)

Malone performing in 2015

According to Malone, he chose "Post Malone" as his [stage name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage_name "Stage name") when he was "14 or 15".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-25) The name was rumored to be a reference to the professional basketball player [Karl Malone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Malone "Karl Malone"),[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-:4-26) but Malone later explained that "Post" is his last name, and he used a "rap name generator" to get "Malone".[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-vh1.com-27)

In 2010, Malone reportedly played guitar in the [metalcore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metalcore "Metalcore") band Ashley's Arrival (also known as Saving Summer) during his high school years. That same year, he auditioned for [Crown the Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_the_Empire "Crown the Empire") as a guitarist. In a 2016 interview, vocalist Andy Leo recalled that Malone broke a guitar string during the audition and was not selected.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-28)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-AsA-1)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-29)

In late 2011, Malone released his oldest known solo project, an 11-track [mixtape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixtape "Mixtape") titled _Manifest Destiny_.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-30)

In 2013, Malone was a member of the band Love In Colors, in which he performed as a vocalist and guitarist.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-LoveInColors-2)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-31)

At age 17, Malone, along with his friend Jazzy Eff, released a parody [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop")[ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_ballad "Sentimental ballad") song called "Why Don't You Love Me" under the alias Leon DeChino, intended for a school project. The song reappeared online in 2016. Malone later referred to the DeChino alias on his song "[Psycho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psycho_(Post_Malone_song) "Psycho (Post Malone song)")".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-33)

At the age of 18, using audio editor [Audacity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audacity_(audio_editor) "Audacity (audio editor)"), Malone released his second mixtape, _Y.A.T.R._, also known as _Youngin' After Them Riches_, in 2014.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-35) He showed it to some of his classmates at [Grapevine High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grapevine_High_School "Grapevine High School").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-rollingstone-22)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-:2-4) He was voted "Most Likely to Become Famous" by his classmates as a senior in high school. He worked at a [Chicken Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicken_Express "Chicken Express") as a teenager.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-rollingstone-22)

Malone later enrolled in [Tarrant County College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarrant_County_College "Tarrant County College"), but dropped out.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-36) After leaving college, Malone moved to Los Angeles with his longtime friend Jason Probst, a professional game streamer.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-39)

After moving to Los Angeles, Malone, Probst, and several other producers and artists formed the music group BLCKVRD and recorded music together.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-40) Several members of the group, including Malone, moved into a house in the [San Fernando Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Fernando_Valley "San Fernando Valley") together. While living in the San Fernando Valley, Malone met record producers [FKi 1st](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FKi_1st "FKi 1st") and Sauce Lord Rich, who formed the production team [FKi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FKi_(production_team) "FKi (production team)"), as well as Rex Kudo, who produced several of Malone's tracks, including "[White Iverson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Iverson "White Iverson")".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-:5-16) Malone recorded the song two days after writing it.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-:2-4) The lyrics of "White Iverson" allude to [Basketball Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naismith_Memorial_Basketball_Hall_of_Fame "Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame") player [Allen Iverson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_Iverson "Allen Iverson").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-:1-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-:3-42)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-:4-26) In February 2015, upon completion, it was uploaded to Malone's SoundCloud account.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-WhiteIversonSC-6) On July 19, 2015, Malone released a [music video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video "Music video") for "White Iverson". The single received praise from rappers [Mac Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mac_Miller "Mac Miller") and [Wiz Khalifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiz_Khalifa "Wiz Khalifa").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-rollingstone-22)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-success-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-44) However the song was mocked by [Earl Sweatshirt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Sweatshirt "Earl Sweatshirt").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone#cite_note-47)
